Rising global interest rates trigger currency depreciation in Pakistan through two channels. As capital flows toward higher-yielding dollar assets, demand for the Pakistani rupee falls while demand for dollars rises. This pushes the rupee's value down against the dollar.

A weaker rupee makes every dollar of external debt more expensive in rupee terms. If the rupee depreciates by 20%, the rupee cost of a dollar-denominated loan repayment increases by the same proportion. This effectively magnifies Pakistan's debt burden without any new borrowing—simply through currency dynamics.

Furthermore, currency depreciation fuels domestic inflation by raising the cost of imports, creating a self-reinforcing cycle: inflation prompts further monetary tightening globally, which causes further capital outflows and rupee depreciation, which drives more domestic inflation.

sections.title: IMF Conditionalities and Fiscal Space
sections.body:
Pakistan's recourse to IMF support during debt crises typically comes with conditionalities that further constrain its policy options. Interest rate hikes demanded by the IMF to control domestic inflation and attract foreign investment conflict with the need for affordable credit for businesses and households. The resulting economic slowdown reduces tax revenues precisely when the government needs additional resources to service its debt.

This tension between debt service obligations, IMF conditionalities, and the need for economic growth represents one of Pakistan's most difficult policy challenges. The country finds itself in a situation where external monetary dynamics beyond its control significantly constrain its domestic policy choices.

sections.title: Pathways to Resilience
sections.body:
Building resilience against global interest rate fluctuations requires Pakistan to pursue several long-term strategies. Reducing dependence on external borrowing through improving domestic revenue mobilization is essential. Expanding the tax base, improving collection efficiency, and reducing leakages would give Pakistan greater fiscal independence.

Diversifying the debt portfolio to include more concessional loans from multilateral sources, exploring local currency financing options, and building adequate foreign exchange reserves are also critical. Additionally, structural reforms that enhance export competitiveness would generate the dollar inflows needed to reduce dependence on debt financing.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Pakistan's debt burden is acutely sensitive to global interest rate dynamics. When major central banks tighten monetary policy, the resulting capital outflows, currency depreciation, and higher borrowing costs create a perfect storm for debt-laden developing economies. For Pakistan, the path forward requires both immediate crisis management and sustained structural reforms to reduce vulnerability to these external monetary shocks that originate in Washington, Frankfurt, and London but are painfully felt in Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad.

publications.title: Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Vulnerability Exposed in an Interconnected World. Analyzing how bottlenecks in global logistics are affecting Pakistan's industries.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries/Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of global supply chains with dramatic clarity. What had previously been an abstract concern for logistics specialists became a visceral reality for manufacturers, retailers, and consumers worldwide. For Pakistan, whose industrial sector—particularly textiles and manufacturing—is deeply integrated into global supply networks, supply chain disruptions represent a significant and recurring threat to economic activity, employment, and export earnings.

sections.title: How Global Supply Chains Work And Fail
sections.body:
Modern manufacturing relies on complex, geographically dispersed supply chains. A textile manufacturer in Pakistan may use cotton from local farms, dyes from China, synthetic fibers from petrochemical producers, specialized machinery from Germany, and finishing chemicals from Europe. This global sourcing strategy optimizes costs but creates multiple points of vulnerability—any disruption anywhere in the chain can halt production.

When the pandemic simultaneously disrupted production at multiple nodes of these chains—as factories closed, workers fell ill, ports became congested, and transport capacity collapsed—the cascading effects spread rapidly across the global economy. Even after immediate production disruptions eased, shipping bottlenecks, container shortages, and logistics backlogs kept supply chains dysfunctional for months.

sections.title: Pakistan's Textile Sector: The Most Exposed
sections.body:
Pakistan's textile sector—which accounts for approximately 60% of the country's export earnings and employs millions—is particularly vulnerable to global supply chain disruptions. While Pakistan produces significant quantities of cotton domestically, the sector depends on imports for man-made fibers, specialized dyes, chemicals, and manufacturing equipment.

During the pandemic-era disruptions, Pakistani textile exporters faced a double challenge. On the supply side, delays and cost increases in imported inputs raised production costs and created uncertainty about delivery timelines. On the demand side, order cancellations by international buyers—particularly in the initial phase of the pandemic when global retail collapsed—left factories with unsold inventory and idle production capacity.

Freight rate increases during the supply chain crisis were dramatic—container shipping rates increased by factors of five to ten in some trade lanes—significantly eroding the competitiveness of Pakistan's exports by raising the landed cost of goods in destination markets.

sections.title: Manufacturing Beyond Textiles
sections.body:
While textiles face the most acute exposure, other manufacturing sectors are also vulnerable. Pakistan's pharmaceutical industry depends on active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and other raw materials largely sourced from China and India. When disruptions in these source countries constrained supply, Pakistan's domestic medicine production faced shortages of essential inputs.

The automotive and electronics assembly sectors, though smaller, depend on imported components and are completely halted when supply chain disruptions prevent the arrival of critical parts. Even Pakistan's construction sector is not immune—import dependencies for steel, specialized equipment, and certain building materials mean that global supply disruptions affect domestic development projects.

sections.title: Structural Vulnerabilities and Opportunities
sections.body:
The supply chain disruptions of the pandemic era revealed Pakistan's structural vulnerability to external shocks while simultaneously creating potential opportunities. As global companies sought to diversify their supply chains away from excessive dependence on single-country sources—particularly China—Pakistan had an opportunity to attract relocated or diversified production capacity.

However, capturing this opportunity required Pakistan to address longstanding competitive weaknesses: high energy costs, unreliable electricity supply, burdensome regulatory frameworks, inadequate logistics infrastructure, and skill gaps in the workforce. The countries that successfully attracted supply chain relocation—Vietnam, Bangladesh, and others—had developed competitive advantages in these areas over years of sustained policy attention.

sections.title: Building Supply Chain Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's approach to building supply chain resilience must operate on multiple levels. At the firm level, businesses can develop more diverse supplier relationships, maintain larger buffer inventories of critical inputs, and invest in process flexibility. At the sector level, industry associations can coordinate to develop alternative sourcing strategies and advocate for policy support.

At the national level, policies that develop domestic capabilities in key input industries reduce import dependence. Improving logistics infrastructure—ports, roads, warehousing, and digital trade facilitation—reduces the impact of external disruptions on domestic production. Trade agreements that provide alternative market access and supply sources enhance resilience.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Global supply chain disruptions have revealed the vulnerability embedded in Pakistan's industrial integration into global networks. The country's textile and manufacturing sectors, while benefiting enormously from global integration in normal times, face severe stress when those networks are disrupted by pandemics, geopolitical conflicts, or natural disasters. Building resilience requires both firm-level adaptations and national policy reforms that address structural weaknesses—ensuring that Pakistan can maintain production and protect livelihoods even when global supply networks are under strain.

publications.title: Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Rising Costs, Shrinking Wallets. An analysis of how global inflationary pressures translate into a domestic crisis in Pakistan.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The world economy is experiencing a significant inflationary wave, with major economies like the United States and the European Union grappling with rising prices across virtually every sector. This global phenomenon is not confined to the borders of advanced economies—it ripples outward, touching developing nations like Pakistan with particularly harsh consequences. For a country already struggling with fiscal imbalances and a fragile economic structure, external inflationary pressures can quickly translate into a crisis of daily survival for millions of citizens.

sections.title: How Global Inflation Reaches Pakistan
sections.body:
Pakistan is a net importer of several essential commodities, including petroleum products, edible oils, industrial raw materials, and machinery. When inflation rises in major economies, the cost of producing and exporting these goods increases. This means Pakistan pays more for the same volume of imports, effectively importing inflation from abroad.

Additionally, the US Dollar's dominant role in global trade means that when the dollar strengthens—as it often does during inflationary periods driven by monetary tightening—Pakistan's rupee buys less in the international market. The result is a compounding effect: higher global prices combined with a weaker domestic currency create a double burden on the Pakistani economy.

sections.title: Impact on Fuel, Food, and Raw Materials
sections.body:
Three sectors feel the impact most acutely. First, fuel: Pakistan is heavily dependent on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). As global energy prices surge—driven by geopolitical tensions, OPEC decisions, and post-pandemic demand rebounds—Pakistan's energy import bill skyrockets. This makes electricity generation, transportation, and industrial production more expensive, cascading into higher prices across the entire economy.

Second, food prices: global food inflation, partly driven by supply chain disruptions, climate events, and conflict zones, raises the cost of imported edible oils, wheat, and pulses. For a country where food constitutes a large portion of household budgets, this directly diminishes the purchasing power of ordinary Pakistanis.

Third, raw materials: industries ranging from textiles to chemicals depend on imported inputs. When these become expensive, production costs rise, leading to either higher prices for consumers or reduced output—neither of which is desirable.

sections.title: The Human Cost
sections.body: The most direct consequence of imported inflation is felt by low- and middle-income households. As prices of everyday essentials—flour, cooking oil, electricity, fuel—climb relentlessly, families find themselves spending a larger fraction of their income just to maintain basic living standards. Savings shrink, debt increases, and poverty rates rise. Pakistan's already stretched social safety nets come under enormous pressure, often proving inadequate to cushion the most vulnerable segments of society.

sections.title: Policy Responses and Their Limitations
sections.body:
The Pakistani government and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) have attempted to manage inflationary pressures through a combination of monetary tightening, subsidies, and import controls. Raising interest rates, for example, can reduce domestic demand and cool inflation but also stifles economic growth and raises the cost of borrowing for businesses and individuals alike.

Subsidies on fuel and food can provide short-term relief but are fiscally unsustainable, especially for a country with limited revenue and a heavy debt burden. Import restrictions may protect foreign exchange reserves in the short run but can lead to shortages and black markets.

Ultimately, Pakistan's capacity to insulate itself from global inflationary waves is constrained by structural vulnerabilities: a narrow export base, low foreign exchange reserves, high import dependence, and limited fiscal space. Addressing these structural issues is essential for building resilience against future inflationary shocks.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The global inflation wave is a sobering reminder of how interconnected today's economies are. For Pakistan, rising international prices translate directly into hardship for its citizens, straining household budgets and government finances alike. While short-term policy measures can offer some relief, the deeper solution lies in structural reforms that reduce import dependence, boost exports, enhance productivity, and build fiscal buffers. Until such reforms take root, Pakistan will remain acutely vulnerable to the economic tides that originate far beyond its borders.

publications.title: Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: How the World's Reserve Currency Shapes Pakistan's Economy. Investigating the impact of a strong US Dollar on the Pakistani Rupee.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The US dollar's role as the world's dominant reserve currency and primary medium of international trade creates a structural asymmetry in the global economy. Countries that earn and hold reserves in dollars benefit from its stability and universal acceptance. Countries like Pakistan that must buy dollars to pay for essential imports and service dollar-denominated debt face a fundamental vulnerability: their economic well-being is significantly influenced by the value of a currency they do not control and a monetary policy set for American domestic conditions.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Rupee Depreciation
sections.body:
The Pakistani rupee's value is determined in foreign exchange markets by the supply and demand for rupees relative to other currencies, particularly the dollar. Several factors create persistent downward pressure on the rupee.

Pakistan's structural trade deficit—importing significantly more than it exports—means that the economy continuously demands more dollars than it earns from exports. This excess demand for dollars creates inherent depreciation pressure. When this deficit is not offset by sufficient inflows of foreign investment, remittances, or borrowing, reserves deplete and the rupee falls.

When the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates, the dollar strengthens globally as international capital flows toward higher-yielding dollar assets. This dollar appreciation is simultaneously rupee depreciation—the mirror image of dollar strength. Thus, American monetary policy decisions intended to address US domestic inflation directly affect Pakistan's exchange rate.

sections.title: The Import Cost Amplification
sections.body:
Currency depreciation creates an immediate and painful amplification of import costs. If Pakistan imports a barrel of oil at $80, and the rupee has depreciated by 20% over a year, the rupee cost of that same barrel has increased by 20%—even if the dollar price of oil remained unchanged.

This mechanism means that Pakistan effectively faces a double burden during periods of global stress: international commodity prices often rise at the same time that the rupee falls, as both are driven by dollar strengthening and global risk aversion. The combination of higher dollar prices and a weaker rupee can dramatically increase the rupee cost of essential imports within a short period, generating intense inflationary pressure.

sections.title: Impact on Businesses and Consumers
sections.body:
The business community faces multiple challenges from currency depreciation. Importers see their costs rise immediately when the rupee depreciates. Manufacturers who use imported raw materials face rising input costs, which they must either absorb—reducing profit margins—or pass on to consumers, contributing to inflation.

Exporters benefit from rupee depreciation in theory, as their goods become cheaper in international markets in dollar terms. However, if their production costs rise due to imported inputs and higher energy costs (themselves partly driven by import costs), the competitive gain is offset. The net benefit to exporters depends on their specific cost structure and the degree to which they can expand production at lower cost in dollar terms.

For consumers, currency depreciation is experienced as higher prices across virtually the entire basket of goods and services. From fuel prices at petrol stations to the cost of electronics, medicines, and processed foods—the depreciated rupee makes everything more expensive.

sections.title: The Political Economy of Exchange Rate Management
sections.body:
Managing the exchange rate involves difficult political choices. Artificially maintaining an overvalued exchange rate by intervening in currency markets to support the rupee can provide temporary relief from import cost increases but depletes foreign exchange reserves and creates distortions that ultimately require more painful correction.

Allowing market-determined exchange rate adjustments as required under IMF programs is often more economically rational but politically contentious given its immediate inflationary impact. Pakistani governments have historically alternated between periods of exchange rate suppression and sharp devaluations, each creating its own set of economic distortions and hardships.

sections.title: Reducing Dollar Vulnerability
sections.body:
Pakistan's long-term vulnerability to dollar dominance can be reduced through several strategies. Building export capacity across diverse sectors generates more dollar earnings domestically, reducing net import demand. Developing domestic production of currently imported goods reduces the dollar demand created by imports.

Diversifying trade and financing relationships—including increasing use of local currencies in bilateral trade with neighboring countries like China and the Gulf states—reduces, at the margin, the exclusive dominance of the dollar in Pakistan's international transactions. Building adequate foreign exchange reserves provides a buffer against short-term pressure without requiring immediate adjustment.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The dollar's dominance in global trade and finance creates a structural challenge for Pakistan that cannot be resolved through exchange rate policy alone. Currency depreciation is both a symptom of underlying economic imbalances and a cause of further inflation and financial stress. Addressing Pakistan's currency vulnerability requires the hard work of structural economic transformation—building exports, reducing import dependence, improving fiscal discipline, and creating the conditions for stable, growth-enabling investment flows.

publications.title: Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Living on the Front Lines of a Global Crisis. How international climate agreements are shaping Pakistan's economic landscape.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Pakistan stands at a painful paradox in the global climate crisis. Despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, the country ranks consistently among the world's most vulnerable nations to the physical impacts of climate change. Extreme heat waves, devastating floods, glacial lake outburst floods, drought, and crop failures are no longer theoretical future scenarios—they are lived realities that are already reshaping Pakistan's economy and threatening its development trajectory.

sections.title: The Physical Reality of Climate Impacts
sections.body:
Pakistan's geographical position makes it acutely sensitive to climate variability. The 2022 super-floods—described by scientists as made significantly more likely and severe by climate change—provide the starkest illustration. These floods inundated approximately one-third of the country's land mass, killed over 1,700 people, displaced millions, destroyed critical infrastructure, and caused economic losses estimated at over $30 billion.

Agricultural losses during the 2022 floods were catastrophic: millions of acres of crops destroyed, vast livestock herds lost, and irrigation infrastructure damaged. In a country where agriculture employs approximately 40% of the workforce and contributes around 20% of GDP, such losses have profound ripple effects throughout the economy. Reduced agricultural output drives food price inflation, reduces rural incomes, and increases food import requirements—all adding pressure to an already strained economy.

sections.title: Recurring Climate Shocks and Economic Stability
sections.body:
The 2022 floods were an extreme event but not an isolated one. Pakistan has experienced increasingly frequent and severe climate-related disruptions: intense heat waves that reduce agricultural productivity and worker output, irregular monsoons that affect crop planting and yields, glacial melting that threatens the long-term water security of the Indus Basin, and coastal erosion threatening populated areas in Sindh and Balochistan.

These recurring shocks create an environment of economic uncertainty that discourages investment, disrupts planning, and imposes continuous repair and recovery costs on a country with already limited fiscal resources. The cumulative economic cost of climate impacts—even without considering catastrophic events like the 2022 floods—represents a significant drag on Pakistan's development potential.

sections.title: International Climate Finance and Pakistan
sections.body:
The global discussion on climate finance has created both opportunities and frustrations for Pakistan. Developed countries have pledged billions in climate finance to help developing nations adapt to climate change and transition to cleaner energy—but the delivery of these commitments has been inconsistent and often falls short of pledged amounts.

Following the 2022 floods, Pakistan's advocacy for climate justice and loss-and-damage compensation drew international attention and contributed to the establishment of a Loss and Damage Fund at COP27. Accessing and effectively utilizing climate finance requires Pakistan to develop strong project pipelines, transparent financial management systems, and institutional capacity to negotiate with international climate funds.

sections.title: Global Climate Policies and Pakistan's Exports
sections.body:
Beyond direct physical impacts, global climate policies create important economic implications for Pakistan. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)—which imposes carbon costs on imports from countries without equivalent carbon pricing—threatens to raise the cost of Pakistani exports entering the EU market over time.

Pakistan's export-oriented industries, particularly textiles and leather, will face pressure to document and reduce their carbon footprints to maintain market access in climate-conscious importing countries. This creates both a compliance cost and an investment opportunity—firms that successfully transition to cleaner production processes may gain competitive advantages in premium export markets that reward sustainability credentials.

sections.title: Building Climate Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's national climate strategy must address both adaptation—reducing vulnerability to impacts that are already locked in—and mitigation—reducing emissions as part of the global effort to limit future warming. Adaptation priorities include flood protection infrastructure, drought-resistant crop varieties, efficient irrigation systems, early warning systems, and climate-resilient construction standards.

Mitigation involves transitioning Pakistan's energy sector toward renewables, improving energy efficiency, developing sustainable transportation, and protecting forests. Many of these investments have co-benefits for economic development—renewable energy reduces fuel import bills, efficient irrigation improves agricultural productivity, and forest protection supports rural livelihoods.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Climate change represents an existential economic threat for Pakistan—one that is already manifesting in devastating floods, disrupted agriculture, and increased reliance on international emergency assistance. Pakistan's experience challenges the international community to deliver meaningful climate finance and ambitious emission reductions. Domestically, building climate resilience requires sustained investment, institutional development, and policy coherence across economic sectors. The cost of inaction—measured in recurring disasters, agricultural decline, and development setbacks—far exceeds the investment required for adaptation and mitigation.

publications.title: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Promises, Progress, and Shifting Priorities. An analysis of CPEC's trajectory amidst shifting global economic dynamics.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) was launched with enormous ambition—a flagship project of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) that promised to transform Pakistan's infrastructure, energy sector, and economic connectivity while cementing a strategic partnership between the two neighboring nations. A decade into implementation, CPEC has delivered significant results in certain areas while facing challenges from Pakistan's economic difficulties, changing global dynamics, and shifts in China's own economic priorities.

sections.title: CPEC's Foundational Vision
sections.body:
At its core, CPEC envisions connecting China's landlocked western Xinjiang region to the Arabian Sea through Pakistan's Gwadar port, creating a shorter and more economical route for Chinese trade and energy imports from the Middle East and Africa. For Pakistan, the corridor was meant to address two critical bottlenecks: an acute energy shortage crippling industrial production and an inadequate transportation network limiting economic activity.

The $62 billion investment—though revised figures vary—was structured to deliver energy projects, road and rail upgrades, and special economic zones (SEZs) that would attract industrial investment and create employment. The vision was of a Pakistan transformed into a regional hub of trade and manufacturing.

sections.title: Progress and Achievements
sections.body:
CPEC has delivered tangible results in Pakistan's power sector. Numerous energy projects—coal, solar, and hydropower—have been completed or are operational, adding significant capacity to the national grid. This has reduced, though not eliminated, Pakistan's chronic electricity shortages that had long suppressed industrial output.

Infrastructure investments have improved road connectivity in various corridors, and Gwadar port has seen significant development. These investments have created employment during construction and improved logistics in certain regions. For Pakistan, attracting such large-scale foreign investment at concessional terms was an achievement in itself given the country's challenging business environment.

sections.title: Challenges and Controversies
sections.body:
CPEC has also generated significant controversy and faces serious challenges. Critics have raised concerns about the transparency of contracts, the terms of financing, and the extent to which Pakistani businesses benefit from CPEC projects—noting that many contracts were awarded to Chinese firms with limited local participation.

The debt obligations associated with CPEC projects—including principal repayments and repatriated profits from independent power producers—have contributed to Pakistan's external financial pressures. The promised industrial cooperation through SEZs has been slower to materialize than anticipated, limiting the employment generation and technology transfer that were central to CPEC's developmental promises.

Geopolitical tensions in the region, security challenges—particularly in Balochistan, and inconsistent policy support from successive Pakistani governments have all slowed implementation.

sections.title: China's Changing Economic Priorities
sections.body:
China's own economic situation is evolving in ways that affect CPEC's trajectory. China's growth has moderated from its earlier double-digit rates, and the country is navigating significant internal economic transitions. The BRI overall has faced scrutiny over debt sustainability concerns, and China has become more selective and cautious in its overseas infrastructure investments.

This shift in Chinese priorities, combined with Pakistan's financial difficulties limiting its ability to fulfill obligations and attract complementary investments, means that CPEC's second phase focusing on industrial development has progressed more slowly than initially envisioned. Both countries need to recalibrate expectations and focus on ensuring that existing investments deliver their intended benefits before committing to ambitious new phases.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.body:
For CPEC to fulfill its transformative potential, several conditions are necessary. Pakistan must improve its business environment through regulatory reforms, consistent policy frameworks, and enhanced security—making SEZs genuinely attractive to both Chinese and international investors. Renegotiating the terms of existing energy agreements to reduce their fiscal burden on Pakistan would improve the corridor's overall economic sustainability.

Diversifying CPEC's scope to include more agriculture, technology, and services cooperation alongside physical infrastructure would better leverage Pakistan's comparative advantages. Greater transparency in project contracts and more meaningful participation of Pakistani firms would also address legitimate concerns about the distribution of benefits.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: CPEC remains a vital component of Pakistan's development strategy and a cornerstone of its strategic relationship with China. Despite falling short of its most ambitious initial projections, the corridor has delivered real infrastructure improvements and energy capacity. In a changing global economy where great power competition intensifies and China recalibrates its overseas investments, Pakistan must be a proactive and strategic partner—ensuring that CPEC delivers lasting economic benefits rather than merely creating debt obligations and foreign-dominated enclaves.

publications.title: Introduction to Monetary Economics
publications.author: Atiq Ur Rehman, Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Monetary Economics, 1st Edition. This book will be of interest to teachers and students of monetary economics, money and banking, macroeconomics and monetary policy.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Books/cover-image.png

sections.title: Major Features of this Edition
sections.body:
• Moderated Stylized facts on money demand and supply, and the relationships between monetary policy, inflation, output and unemployment in the economy.
  • Theories on money demand and supply, including precautionary and buffer stock models, and monetary aggregation.
  • Competing macroeconomic models of the Classical and Keynesian paradigms, along with a discussion of their validity and consistency with the stylized facts.
  • Excellent pedagogical features such as introductions, key concepts, end-of-chapter summaries, and review and discussion questions.

sections.title: About the Authors
sections.body:
Dr. Atiq ur Rehman is Associate Professor of Economics at University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, UAJK and has taught monetary economics and macroeconomics for over 15 years.

Dr. Shakeel Shahzad is Assistant Professor of Economics at Bahria University, Islamabad and has taught monetary economics, macroeconomics, and econometrics for over 10 years.

publications.title: The Effect of Various Relationship Factors on Business Success; Empirical Evidence from Business Partners of Pakistan and China
publications.author: Prof. Dr. Attiya Yasmin Javid, Shakeel Shahzad, Jawad Ali
publications.description: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment...
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Reports/The Effect of Various Relationship/Cover-image.png

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment in a sample of business partners from Pakistanis and Chinese companies that do business together in Pakistan. Path modeling was used to explore the hierarchical nature of the relationship dimensions amongst one another and on the dependent variables. We conclude that relationship variables in our cross-cultural study are hierarchical and that personal relationships are critical to building and enhancing inter-organizational relationships. We further noted that some relationship dimensions may not have significant direct relationships with commitment, but their indirect and total effects may be significant. Our results challenge conventional conceptualization of relationship dimensions by suggesting a hierarchy of importance among these dimensions.

  • Performing Organization: Pakistan Institute of Development Economics

publications.title: Role of Remittance’s in Pakistan Economy; Analysis of the current status and guideline for Reforms
publications.author: أ.د. عطية ي. جافيد
publications.description: التقرير النهائي المقدم إلى لجنة التعليم العالي.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Reports/HEC final Report (Prof. Dr. Attiya Y. Javid - 21052020) (1)/Cover-image.png

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body:
Remittances for a very respectable size in the economy of Pakistan, and they form about 8.8% of GDP. These remittances play extremely important in management of Pakistan economy, mainly contributing to the management of current account balance. For a long period over the history, Pakistan is facing large trade deficit and the remittances are used to bring the current account deficit at balance. However, when remittances reach the country through formal channels, the bank keep the foreign currency with them and pay rupee in exchange of it. Thus about Rs. 3.3 trillion come into the pockets of recipients. The earlier studies on remittances show that the marginal propensity to save for the remitters is much higher compared to the overall propensity to save. Supposing marginal propensity to save to be only 20%, the amount of saving should be sufficient to finance millions of jobs. But no job related activities are observable.

The first question arises that how remittances contribute to the economy? A model was estimated using WALS approach which show that the huge surge in remittances didn’t effect the pace of growth of economy.

The second question that arises is; what is happening to the remittances that they don’t contribute to economy. Extensive Survey was carried out in selected cities of all four provinces, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad Capital territory and Gilgit Baltistan to find the answer to this question. The findings reveal that largest share of the investable part of remittances goes into real estate, especially sale and purchase of plots which is extremely capital intensive business and one doesn’t contribute to the employment generation and any other economic benefit.

The next important question was to recommend the measures for enhancing the flow of remittances through formal channels and to recommend measures for welfare of remittances. We propose that in order to increase the formal inflow, SBP should subsidize the formal inflow. This subsidy would be proportional to size of remittances and would not be directly encashable. Half of this subsidy is deposited to the premium for health and life insurance of the remitter and his/her family and remaining half of subsidy is to be deposited to a welfare fund for remitter. The amount deposited to the fund along with the profit would be payable to the remitter when he/she quits overseas job, or when he/she intends to finance the business of any of his heirs. Such a subsidy would be a goodwill gesture from the government for the remitters and would help remitters to start a business when he/she comes back to the homeland. Since this subsidy would not be directly encashable, it would not affect the current exchange rate.

The last and most important question was; how to utilize the remittances in better way. We have found from the data we collected that the major chunk of investable remittances goes into real estate and in particular, business of plots. This is extremely capital intensive business and we have to replace it with some labor intensive business. We argue that the investable part of remittances can be invested in the mega-development projects using bonds issued in the name of projects. The investors may be paid return when the project become mature. We argue that such an investment must be protected through proper legislation. We also discuss the necessary measures needed to make such investments viable.

publications.title: Cybersecurity Challenges in Digital Tax Systems: Protecting Revenue, Trust, and Citizens
publications.author: Shehzad Khan (Software Engineer and Analyst)
publications.description: Cybersecurity Challenges in Digital Tax Systems: Protecting Revenue, Trust, and Citizens explores the growing cybersecurity risks associated with modern digital tax platforms and highlights why securing taxpayer data has become essential for governments, businesses, and citizens alike. The blog examines key challenges including data privacy, identity theft, phishing attacks, system vulnerabilities, third-party supply chain risks, and the balance between regulatory compliance and user-friendly digital services. It also provides practical recommendations such as implementing multi-factor authentication, encrypting sensitive data, strengthening vendor security, adopting risk-based access controls, and improving incident response planning. Ultimately, the blog emphasizes that cybersecurity is not merely a technical issue but a shared responsibility that is critical for protecting public trust, ensuring uninterrupted tax services, and building resilient digital tax ecosystems for the future.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Cybersecurity Challenges in Digital Tax Systems/Cybersecurity Challenges in Digital Tax Systems.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Digital tax systems have become a backbone of modern government, collecting revenue, distributing refunds, and enabling everything from online filing to real-time reporting. But the same digitization that makes tax administration faster and more convenient also creates an attractive target: a single breach can expose millions of identities, disrupt essential services, and undermine confidence in public institutions.

In this blog, you’ll learn the biggest cybersecurity challenges facing digital tax platforms, data privacy, identity theft, phishing and fraud, system vulnerabilities, third-party risk, regulatory compliance, and the constant trade-off between usability and security, plus practical ways governments, businesses, and taxpayers can improve resilience.

sections.title: 1) Data privacy: tax data is a high-value, high-impact target
sections.body:
Tax systems concentrate some of the most sensitive information a person or organization has: names, addresses, national identifiers, bank details, income history, dependents, and sometimes healthcare or benefits data. That depth makes breaches uniquely damaging not just embarrassing, but financially and socially disruptive.

  • Scale and centralization: A single platform may hold records for an entire country or region, multiplying blast radius when security controls fail.
  • Secondary harm: Exposed tax records can fuel downstream crime: account takeover, SIM swaps, fraudulent loans, and targeted scams that reference personal details to look “legitimate.”
  • Data sharing and analytics: Modern compliance efforts often connect tax data to payroll, customs, social security, and benefits systems. Each integration increases the number of pathways an attacker can exploit and complicates privacy governance.

Resilience recommendations:

  • Minimize and segment: Collect only what’s needed, separate sensitive fields, and limit who (and what services) can access them.
  • Encrypt everywhere: Strong encryption at rest and in transit, plus robust key management and rotation practices.
  • Design for privacy: build consent, retention limits, and auditability into system requirements rather than bolting them on after deployment.

sections.title: 2) Identity theft: refunds, credits, and stolen credentials are a perfect storm
sections.body:
Digital tax platforms are prime territory for identity theft because the attacker’s payoff can be immediate. Fraudsters don’t always need to “steal money from the government" directly, often they file a return early using stolen data, redirect refunds, or hijack an online account to change bank details.

For governments, identity theft leads to financial losses, costly investigations, and delayed refunds for legitimate citizens. For taxpayers, it means months of paperwork, frozen accounts, and the stress of proving you are you. Businesses are affected too: employee data stolen from payroll or HR systems can be used to file fraudulent individual returns, and compromised business accounts can enable false claims or the manipulation of filings.

AttackWhat it looks like in tax systemsImpact
Account takeoverCredential stuffing, password resets via hijacked email/SMS, or session theftRefund diversion, profile changes, locked-out taxpayers
Synthetic identityBlending real and fake data to create “new” filers or entitiesFraudulent refunds/credits; harder detection
Insider misuseUnauthorized access by staff or contractorsTargeted leaks, fraud enablement, reputational damage

Resilience recommendations:

  • Stronger authentication: Adopt multi-factor authentication (MFA) that resists interception (for example, app-based or hardware-backed approaches) and protect account recovery flows as carefully as logins.
  • Behaviour and risk signals: Flag unusual device/location patterns, repeated failed attempts, abnormal filing speed, or high-risk bank changes; step up verification when risk increases.
  • Refund controls: Add friction to high-risk transactions (like first-time bank accounts) while keeping normal refunds smooth for trusted users.

sections.title: 3) Phishing and fraud: The human layer is still the easiest way in
sections.body:
Even the best-designed systems can be undermined by social engineering. Attackers impersonate tax authorities, payroll providers, or internal finance teams to trick people into giving up credentials, approving fraudulent changes, or installing malware. Tax season creates a predictable spike in urgency and anxiety, conditions that scammers exploit with “your refund is ready” or “final notice” messages.

The business audience sees this in two ways: employees receive convincing emails that target payroll and finance systems, and customers receive messages that look like official communications. The more legitimate digital services become, the more believable impersonation gets, especially when criminals can reference real leaked data (names, prior addresses, employers) to personalize the lure.

Warning sign — The most effective phishing attempts don’t ask for “passwords.” They ask for a small action that feels routine: “Confirm your bank details,” “Download your tax document,” or “Approve this payroll update.”

Resilience recommendations:

  • Secure communications: Provide a single, consistent official channel (in-app inbox or portal) for sensitive messages, and encourage taxpayers to avoid links in emails/SMS.
  • Anti-fraud playbooks: Define how to handle suspected scams: rapid takedown requests, public advisories, call center scripts, and escalation paths.
  • Training that matches reality: Short, frequent training focused on the exact workflows people use (payroll updates, vendor payments, account recovery), not generic “spot the phish” posters.
  • Detection and monitoring: Monitor for lookalike domains, unusual email patterns, bot traffic, and spikes in password reset attempts during filing peaks.

sections.title: 4) System vulnerabilities: Legacy platforms, fast change, and the risk of “one missed patch”
sections.body:
Digital tax systems often sit at the intersection of legacy infrastructure and rapid policy change. New credits, reporting obligations, and integration requirements can arrive on tight timelines, increasing the risk of rushed deployments and incomplete testing. Meanwhile, older components may be difficult to patch, hard to monitor, or dependent on out-of-date libraries and operating systems. This creates familiar technical risk patterns with very real public outcomes: an exploited vulnerability can trigger service outages at peak filing time, expose records through misconfigurations, or allow an attacker to pivot from a public portal into internal systems.

Common vulnerability hotspots:

  • Web application weaknesses: Injection flaws, broken access control, insecure file uploads, and API vulnerabilities in portals and integrations.
  • Configuration drift: Inconsistent settings across environments, overly permissive storage buckets, or logging left disabled after troubleshooting.
  • Availability threats: Denial-of-service attacks timed for deadlines; capacity constraints that behave like outages even without an attacker.

sections.title: 5) Third-party and supply-chain risk: vendors extend your attack surface
sections.body:
Tax ecosystems rarely run on a single platform. Governments rely on cloud providers, software integrators, identity services, call centers, print/mail vendors, analytics tools, and sometimes outsourced development teams. Businesses rely on accounting suites, payroll platforms, and tax preparers. Each third party introduces new access paths, new data flows, and new dependencies—meaning your security is only as strong as the weakest link in the chain.

Supply-chain incidents can be especially damaging because they bypass traditional perimeter defenses. If a trusted provider is compromised, malicious updates or stolen credentials can give attackers a legitimate-looking route into sensitive systems.

Third-party risk areaWhat can go wrongWhat “good” looks like
AccessOver-privileged vendor accounts; shared credentialsLeast privilege, unique identities, time-bound access
Data handlingUnclear retention; weak encryption; shadow copiesContractual controls, encryption, clear deletion/retention
Software supply chainCompromised updates; unsafe dependenciesSigned builds, dependency scanning, secure release processes
Operational resilienceVendor outage becomes public outageSLAs, redundancy, tested contingency plans

Resilience recommendations:

  • Vendor due diligence with teeth: Validate security controls, incident response maturity, and audit rights; reassess regularly, not just at procurement.
  • Zero-trust access patterns: Limit network reach, isolate environments, and monitor vendor sessions with strong logging and alerts.
  • Exit and continuity plans: Assume a key provider can fail; plan how services continue during outages or contract transitions.

sections.title: 6) Compliance and usability: Meeting the rules without breaking the experience
sections.body:
Digital tax systems operate under strict legal and regulatory obligations: privacy laws, data localization rules, records retention requirements, and sector-specific security standards. Compliance is essential—but compliance alone doesn’t guarantee security. A system can “Tick the boxes” while still being vulnerable to modern attack techniques, or while creating user experiences so painful that people look for workarounds.

This is where the tension between usability and security becomes most visible. Strong verification reduces fraud, but if it blocks legitimate users, especially people without consistent phone access, stable addresses, or modern devices, it can reduce adoption and increase the burden on in-person services. On the other hand, making portals frictionless can invite automated attacks and large-scale abuse.

Key takeaway: The goal isn’t “maximum security at any cost.” It’s risk-based security: stronger checks when the risk is higher, smoother paths when confidence is high.

Resilience recommendations:

  • Risk-based identity journeys: Combine multiple signals (device, behaviour, document checks, known history) instead of relying on a single factor like SMS codes.
  • Accessible alternatives: Provide secure fallback paths for users who can’t complete digital verification, with clear timelines and minimal friction.
  • Audit-ready by design: Maintain clear logs, change histories, and data lineage so compliance reporting doesn’t require risky ad-hoc access to production systems.
  • Measure what matters: Track fraud rates, false positives, call center deflection, and user drop-off to tune controls without guessing.

sections.title: Conclusion: Resilience is a shared responsibility
sections.body:
Digital tax systems sit where money, identity, and public trust intersect. That makes cybersecurity failures uniquely expensive: they can drain revenue, delay refunds, disrupt filing seasons, and expose citizens and businesses to long-term harm. The biggest risks tend to cluster around predictable pressure points, sensitive data concentration, identity-based fraud, social engineering, unpatched vulnerabilities, vendor dependencies, and the constant balancing act between security and usability.

If you’re responsible for a tax platform, a finance function, or an ecosystem that touches tax data, the best next step is to turn “security awareness” into a short, measurable plan. Pick a few high-impact improvements, assign owners, and test them before peak filing periods.

Practical call to action: A 30-day resilience checklist

  • Review what tax data you store, where it lives, and who can access it; remove or reduce anything non-essential.
  • Harden account security: MFA for staff and privileged users, stronger recovery flows, and alerts for bank-detail changes.
  • Run a phishing and impersonation drill tailored to tax-season scenarios (refund notices, payroll updates, “urgent” compliance requests).
  • Patch and test: prioritize internet-facing systems and critical APIs; validate logging and monitoring coverage end-to-end.
  • Map third-party access and data sharing; enforce least privilege and confirm incident notification timelines in contracts.
  • Define a peak-season incident plan (including comms): what you'll do in the first 60 minutes of a suspected breach or outage.

publications.title: AI vs Tax Fraud: How Intelligent Systems Can Detect Fake Transactions
publications.author: Shehzad Khan (Software Engineer and Analyst)
publications.description: AI vs Tax Fraud: How Intelligent Systems Can Detect Fake Transactions explores how artificial intelligence is transforming tax enforcement in Pakistan by identifying fraudulent invoices, ghost suppliers, and suspicious transaction networks. The blog explains how AI-powered analytics, e-invoicing, anomaly detection, and network analysis help the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) detect tax fraud more quickly and accurately while supporting honest taxpayers. It also highlights Pakistan's ongoing digital tax reforms, the benefits of data-driven compliance, and the challenges of implementation, including data quality, governance, and cybersecurity. The article concludes that combining AI with transparent policies and robust digital infrastructure can strengthen tax compliance, increase government revenue, and create a fairer and more efficient tax system for Pakistan.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/AI vs Tax Fraud - How Intelligent Systems Can Detect Fake Transactions/AI vs Tax Fraud - How Intelligent Systems Can Detect Fake Transactions.jpg

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Pakistan’s tax system faces a persistent integrity problem: fraudulent or manipulated transactions, especially in sales tax, reduce revenue, distort competition, and undermine fiscal stability. Over 2024–2026, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and the Government of Pakistan have accelerated reforms around digital invoicing (e-invoicing), data integration, and AI-assisted risk analytics, priorities also emphasized in programme and development partner documentation (IMF; World Bank; ADB).

In this blog we explain how fake transactions work, how AI-enabled systems detect them in practice, and what Pakistan’s reform direction implies, while separating confirmed measures from unknowns.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.body:
Tax fraud is deliberate evasion of tax due or unlawful claiming of refunds/credits. In transaction-based taxes, it often relies on invoices that do not reflect real economic activity. Common schemes include:

  • Fake / flying invoices: invoices for sales/purchases that did not occur, often to inflate input tax credits or reduce taxable income.
  • Ghost suppliers: shell entities that issue invoices without real capacity (“invoice printers”).
  • Circular trading: invoice loops that simulate trade to generate artificial credits/refunds.

These schemes are harder to sustain when verification is near real-time and data is integrated across buyer–seller chains.

sections.title: Why it Matters in Pakistan
sections.body:
Pakistan’s fiscal challenge is structural: revenue remains low relative to spending needs. IMF programme reporting places general government tax revenue around ~10–11% of GDP in FY2024–FY2025 (with FBR revenue lower than the overall tax ratio). (IMF staff reports: IMF eLibrary).

In that context, invoice fraud is not a niche compliance issue: it weakens sales tax integrity, disrupts refunds, and penalises firms that document activity and pay due tax.

sections.title: Who is Affected
sections.body:
Invoice fraud leaks resources that are vital for the country's development, impact is shared by:

  • Government: revenue leakage increases deficits and borrowing needs, reducing fiscal flexibility.
  • Compliant businesses: unfair competition rewards those using fake invoices or suppressed reporting.
  • Workers and consumers: weak revenue often translates into underfunded services and heavier reliance on easy-to-collect taxes.

sections.title: Current Situation in Pakistan (2024–2026)
sections.body:
Pakistan’s compliance modernisation is moving toward near-real-time transaction visibility and risk-based intervention. Key elements referenced in official sources include:

  • E-invoicing: phased integration requirements for registered businesses, enabling faster cross-checks. (FBR Portal)
  • AI-assisted audit selection: reported use of analytics to prioritise higher-risk cases and standardise workflows. (FBR Publications)
  • Analytics to block suspicious claims: Ministry of Finance reporting cites instances of sales tax claims blocked through analytics. (Ministry of Finance)

The cautious conclusion is: Pakistan has moved from policy intent to operational deployment in e-invoicing and analytics; durable gains depend on coverage, data quality, and governance.

sections.title: Comparison of Control Approaches
sections.body:
Effective enforcement requires a balance of speed, coverage, and adaptability. The table below compares historical manual approaches with modern intelligent systems.

Control ApproachWhat it looks likeStrengths & Limits
Manual, after-the-fact auditReturns reviewed later; sampling; document requestsStrength: deep review of a few cases.
Limit: slow; networks can adapt quickly.
Rule-based digital checksValidations and thresholds on filing and invoice fieldsStrength: consistent.
Limit: fraud adapts to fixed rules.
AI + e-invoicingAnomaly and network signals plus faster buyer–seller matchingStrength: faster detection at scale.
Limit: requires strong data and due process.

sections.title: How AI Detects Fake Transactions
sections.body:
AI is not a single tool; it is a set of methods that helps a tax authority prioritise verification. Effective systems combine models, rules, human review, and legal process.

  • Anomaly detection: Models flag unusual claims relative to peers or a taxpayer’s own history — for example, input credits that are out of line with sector patterns or sudden spikes in refunds. The output should be a prompt for checks, not automatic penalties.
  • Network (graph) analytics: Because fake invoicing is often networked, graph analytics can highlight circular trading structures and “invoice-printer” hubs (many buyers linked to weak-capacity suppliers). This is particularly relevant where credits/refunds depend on chains of invoices, not a single document.

sections.title: E-Invoicing as a Control Mechanism
sections.body:
E-invoicing changes the enforcement timeline by enabling earlier cross-checks. A simplified flow is:

  • Seller issues an approved digital invoice (often via ERP/POS integration).
  • The system validates core fields and matches counterparties where possible.
  • Risk signals route higher-risk cases for verification (including refund controls).

Pakistan’s reform direction aligns with this approach: phased integration plus analytics-driven workflows. (FBR: fbr.gov.pk; IMF: elibrary.imf.org)

sections.title: Document Intelligence for Screening
sections.body: Where refunds and disputes involve scanned documents and narrative text, OCR and language tools can extract fields and flag inconsistencies. These tools are best treated as triage support rather than final decision-makers.

sections.title: Economic and Administrative Impact
sections.body:
Fraudulent transactions reduce collections and also create second-order costs: distorted competition, pressure to tighten refunds, and weaker fiscal credibility. Where the Ministry of Finance reports “blocked” suspicious claims, the implication is operational impact — but “blocked” values typically represent a lower bound on attempted fraud. (Pakistan Economic Survey: finance.gov.pk)

Administratively, digitisation can reduce discretion and improve audit trails, but transitional costs remain (integration work for firms, staff training, and model calibration to limit false positives).

sections.title: Legal and Policy Background
sections.body:
Pakistan’s shift toward technology-led compliance is grounded in a mix of administrative rules, enforcement policy, and programme-linked reforms. Public sources consistently reference:

  • E-invoicing mandates and operational guidance: Scope, timelines, and integration requirements. (FBR: fbr.gov.pk)
  • Risk-based audit selection: Reported use of analytics to focus scrutiny where risk is higher. (FBR: download1.fbr.gov.pk)
  • Revenue mobilisation as a reform priority: Reflected in IMF reporting and development partner framing of domestic revenue mobilisation and digitalisation. (IMF: elibrary.imf.org; World Bank: worldbank.org)

The policy implication is straightforward: stronger digital controls require clear authority, due process, and taxpayer service, otherwise compliance becomes automated friction.

sections.title: Hidden Challenges and Risks
sections.body:
The limiting factors are typically execution and governance:

  • Data quality and identity resolution: inconsistent identifiers and classification increase noise and false positives.
  • Coverage gaps: weak links outside integrated invoicing can absorb and route fraud.
  • Model governance and proportionality: monitoring bias, recalibration, and human review for high-impact actions (e.g., refund holds).
  • Cybersecurity and resilience: as integration expands, the tax system becomes critical infrastructure. (Government communications: pid.gov.pk)

sections.title: International Comparison
sections.body: International practice broadly supports the same lesson: e-invoicing and analytics can reduce sales tax/VAT fraud when coverage is broad, standards are consistent, and enforcement is paired with due process and service. (OECD: oecd.org)

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.body:
To reduce fake transactions while improving legitimate compliance outcomes, policymakers should:

  • Scale e-invoicing where risk is highest: prioritise invoice-chaining and refund-exposed segments using phased onboarding and clear standards.
  • Publish a small transparency set: coverage/volume indicators, refund processing time, and aggregated blocked suspicious claims (without exposing detection rules).
  • Fix “data plumbing” first: standardise master data and improve matching to reduce false positives.
  • Strengthen model and decision governance: audit logs, bias monitoring, recalibration, and clear appeal pathways.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Progress is credible when fake claims become harder to execute, legitimate refunds become faster and more predictable, and compliant firms face fewer arbitrary disputes. By combining AI with transparent policies and robust digital infrastructure, Pakistan can strengthen tax compliance, increase government revenue, and build a fairer and more efficient tax system.

publications.title: The Role of Mobile Applications in Improving Taxpayer Services and Compliance
publications.author: Sarfaraz Ahmed (Economics and Policy Analyst)
publications.description: Mobile technology is transforming how citizens interact with public institutions, and tax administration is no exception. In Pakistan, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has embraced this shift through digital tools like the Tax Asaan App, allowing taxpayers to register, file returns, check Active Taxpayer List (ATL) status, and verify tax information — all from their phones.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/The Role of Mobile Applications in Improving Taxpayer Services and Compliance/The Role of Mobile Applications in Improving Taxpayer Services and Compliance.jpg

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Mobile applications are transforming public services worldwide, including tax administration. In Pakistan, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has introduced digital services such as the Tax Asaan App to make tax-related processes more convenient. Mobile apps help taxpayers access services, submit returns, verify tax status, and receive updates, improving compliance and transparency.

This convenience is more than a nice-to-have; it's a compliance strategy. As Pakistan works to widen its tax net, mobile access is proving key to greater transparency, efficiency, and trust between citizens and FBR.

sections.title: FRPD Analysis
sections.body:
Facts:

  • FBR has launched mobile applications like Tax Asaan to simplify tax services.
  • Taxpayers can register, file returns, check Active Taxpayer List (ATL) status, and verify tax information through mobile apps.
  • Digital services reduce paperwork and save time.

Research:

Studies show that mobile tax applications improve taxpayer satisfaction by making tax services more accessible and user-friendly. Countries with digital tax systems often experience higher tax compliance, lower administrative costs, and greater transparency.

Policy Recommendations:

  • Expand mobile app features for all tax services.
  • Improve app security and user experience.
  • Promote digital literacy through awareness campaigns.
  • Integrate mobile payment options for easier tax payments.

Development Outlook:

  • Increase voluntary tax compliance.
  • Reduce tax evasion and administrative delays.
  • Enhance taxpayer trust in FBR, support Pakistan's digital economy, and increase government revenue.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Mobile applications are becoming an essential tool for modern tax administration. By improving accessibility, convenience, and transparency, they encourage taxpayers to comply with tax laws. Continued investment in secure and user-friendly mobile tax services can strengthen Pakistan's tax system and contribute to sustainable economic development.

publications.title: Filer vs Non-Filer in Pakistan: Benefits, Risks, and the Future of Tax Compliance
publications.author: Shehzad Khan (Software Engineer and Analyst)
publications.description: With Pakistan’s tax net still narrow and compliance a national priority, the filer vs non-filer divide has become more than a technical label — it is now a central policy tool shaping how the state collects revenue, how businesses plan, and how citizens interact with the formal economy.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Filer vs Non-Filer in Pakistan - Benefits, Risks, and the Future of Tax Compliance/Filer vs Non-Filer in Pakistan - Benefits, Risks, and the Future of Tax Compliance.jpg

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The distinction between a filer and a non-filer has become one of the most consequential ideas in Pakistan’s tax system. In theory, it rewards documentation and penalizes those outside the tax net. In practice, it has helped the state raise some revenue and nudge people toward filing, but it has also created complexity, distortions, and administrative burden. The latest filing data shows that Pakistan recorded 5.9 million income tax return filings for Tax Year 2025, a 17.6% increase year-on-year. That is a meaningful improvement. But the larger policy question remains unresolved: does a compliance system built around withholding penalties and status categories create a durable tax culture, or does it simply push transactions into more opaque channels?

This article examines why the filer vs non-filer framework exists, what benefits it offers, where it falls short, how it affects businesses and taxpayers, and what the future may look like as Pakistan moves toward digital invoicing, faceless assessment, and more risk-based enforcement. Where recent reform is still in policy direction rather than final implementation, that distinction is stated clearly.

sections.title: Background: What Filer and Non-Filer Mean
sections.body:
In Pakistan, a filer is a person or business that appears on the Active Taxpayers List, commonly known as the ATL, after filing a return for the relevant tax year. The ATL is updated weekly, on Mondays. A non-filer is someone who has not filed the relevant return and therefore faces higher withholding tax rates on a range of transactions. These can include banking activity, property transactions, vehicle-related payments, contracts, and some business payments. The idea is simple: if you do not document your income, you pay more at the point of transaction.

A new late filer category was introduced in Budget 2026. Based on the policy direction discussed publicly, it adds a PKR 25,000 surcharge for filing after the deadline and applies withholding rates that sit between filer and non-filer treatment. Because implementation details can evolve, the category should be viewed as a policy shift toward stronger filing discipline rather than a final, settled endpoint.

sections.title: Current Situation in Pakistan
sections.body:
Pakistan’s current tax environment reflects both progress and strain. On the progress side, 5.9 million income tax return filings for Tax Year 2025 show that the system is drawing in more returns than before. On the strain side, the broader structure still relies heavily on withholding taxes, which means the state often collects through transactions rather than through a broad, fully documented income base.

The policy debate has intensified around phasing out the non-filer category altogether and simplifying the compliance framework. That debate is not new, but it has gained momentum as digital enforcement tools become more available and as institutions such as the IMF, PIDE, World Bank, OECD, ADB, SBP, PBS, Ministry of Finance, UNDP, and the World Economic Forum continue to shape the wider discussion on tax modernization, documentation, and digital governance. Recent policy direction also points toward digital invoicing, faceless assessment, automated audit concepts, and risk-based enforcement. These measures suggest that the tax administration is trying to move from a status-based system toward a data-driven one, though full implementation remains a work in progress.

sections.title: Main Challenges in the Filer vs Non-Filer System
sections.body:
The filer vs non-filer model has several structural problems:

  • It can penalize transactions rather than actual income.
  • It encourages compliance in form, but not always in substance.
  • It adds administrative complexity for taxpayers and the tax authority.
  • It can distort pricing and behavior in banking, property, automobiles, and services.
  • It may widen the gap between formal rules and informal economic practice.

At a policy level, the real challenge is not only to get more people on the ATL, but to make filing simpler, more accurate, and more meaningful as a signal of economic activity.

sections.title: Root Causes of Low Tax Compliance
sections.body:
Pakistan’s compliance problem is not explained by one factor alone. It reflects a combination of structural and behavioral constraints:

  • A narrow tax base that places pressure on those already visible to the system.
  • A large informal economy that remains difficult to document consistently.
  • Heavy reliance on withholding taxes as a practical collection tool.
  • Complex rules, changing procedures, and inconsistent taxpayer understanding.
  • Limited trust between taxpayers and institutions.
  • A cash-heavy environment that slows the move toward traceable transactions.

These root causes matter because they explain why the filer vs non-filer structure persists. It is easier to tax visible transactions than to fully document income that moves through informal channels.

sections.title: Economic Impact
sections.body:
The system has both short-term and long-term economic consequences. In the short term, higher withholding on non-filers can raise revenue and encourage some people to enter the tax system. It also gives the government an immediate collection tool in a difficult environment. But the longer-term effects are more complicated. Transaction-based penalties can discourage formal activity, push people toward informal intermediaries, and create incentives to structure deals in ways that avoid detection. The result is often partial compliance rather than full documentation.

That is why institutions such as the IMF and World Bank tend to emphasize broader tax base expansion, digitization, and simpler administration over heavily segmented compliance regimes. The policy logic is not just to collect more, but to collect more efficiently and with fewer distortions.

sections.title: Impact on Businesses
sections.body:
For businesses, filer status can materially affect operating costs and planning decisions.

AreaFilerNon-Filer
Withholding taxLower rates on many transactionsHigher rates across many transactions
Access to banking and servicesSmoother compliance profileMore friction and higher transaction costs
Administrative burdenReturn filing and documentation still requiredAdditional tax cost plus pressure to regularize later

For a compliant business, filer status can improve predictability and credibility with banks, suppliers, and regulators. For a non-filer, the system raises cost, complicates transactions, and may increase the incentive to operate through proxies or informal arrangements.

sections.title: Impact on Taxpayers
sections.body:
For individual taxpayers, the main benefit of filer status is lower withholding and better access to formal financial services. In practical terms, that can mean lower tax on property-related transactions, easier dealings with banks, and a clean compliance record.

The risk for non-filers is not only higher withholding. It is also uncertainty. Taxpayers may face notices, difficulty proving the source of income, or pressure to regularize several years at once. For many households, the issue is not deliberate evasion but confusion about filing obligations, especially when salary tax has already been withheld. In simple terms, the filer label functions like a compliance credential. But when the system becomes too complicated, it can discourage people from filing at all, which is the opposite of the policy goal.

sections.title: Government Perspective
sections.body:
From the government’s point of view, the filer vs non-filer system is a practical response to a difficult revenue environment. Pakistan’s tax administration must operate with limited documentation, a large informal economy, and strong pressure to improve collections without disrupting the economy. That explains why the Ministry of Finance, FBR, and related institutions have leaned on a mix of enforcement, digitization, and procedural tightening.

The current direction includes digital invoicing, faceless assessment, automated audit concepts, and stronger risk-based enforcement. These measures are designed to improve compliance without relying entirely on physical contact or discretionary intervention. The policy challenge is balancing revenue needs with credibility. If the system is seen mainly as punitive, resistance grows. If it is seen as predictable, fair, and data-driven, compliance becomes more sustainable.

sections.title: International Best Practices
sections.body:
International experience suggests that strong tax systems do not depend on multiple taxpayer categories with widely different transaction costs. Instead, they tend to rely on simplicity, broad coverage, and digital traceability.

Policy principleInternational practiceRelevance for Pakistan
SimplicityFewer special categories and clearer rulesWould reduce confusion and filing friction
Digital reportingE-invoicing, real-time data, automated checksSupports documentation and audit accuracy
Risk-based enforcementFocus on high-risk cases rather than blanket pressureMore efficient than broad status penalties
Voluntary complianceTrust, service, and predictability matterCould improve filing behavior over time

This is why organizations such as the OECD and ADB often stress administrative simplicity, while the IMF and World Bank emphasize broader revenue mobilization through better systems rather than more complexity. The lesson for Pakistan is not to copy any one country, but to build a system that is easier to understand and harder to evade.

sections.title: Digital Transformation Opportunities
sections.body:
Digital reform offers Pakistan the chance to move beyond the filer/non-filer divide. The key opportunity is to make compliance based on verified activity rather than on status alone. Possible gains include:

  • Unified taxpayer identity across systems.
  • Digital invoicing that improves transaction traceability.
  • Real-time data integration across agencies where legally and operationally possible.
  • Faster compliance checks and fewer manual delays.
  • Better targeting of enforcement toward material risks.

If these reforms mature, the system could reduce dependence on broad withholding penalties and gradually replace them with more transparent, data-led administration.

sections.title: AI and Technology Opportunities
sections.body:
AI and analytics can strengthen tax administration if used carefully and transparently. The most promising uses are not glamorous; they are practical.

  • Risk scoring for audit selection.
  • Mismatch detection between income, assets, and declared activity.
  • Anomaly detection in invoices and transaction patterns.
  • Taxpayer support tools that explain filing steps in plain language.
  • Better prioritization of enforcement against repeated non-compliance.

The value of AI is not to replace judgment. It is to help the tax administration focus limited capacity where the risk is highest. That is especially important in a system with a narrow tax base and a large informal sector.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.body:
Pakistan’s tax system would benefit from a gradual but deliberate shift away from status-based penalties toward simpler, data-supported compliance. Key actions include:

  • Simplify withholding categories so that taxpayer treatment is easier to understand.
  • Phase out the non-filer category over time, if digital coverage and enforcement capacity continue to improve.
  • Expand digital invoicing and other traceability tools in a phased, practical manner.
  • Use faceless and risk-based assessment more widely to reduce discretion and improve fairness.
  • Invest in taxpayer education so filing is seen as manageable, not intimidating.
  • Target willful evasion more aggressively than minor procedural mistakes.
  • Improve service quality, refunds, and communication so compliance feels worthwhile.
  • Coordinate across institutions where data sharing is lawful, secure, and useful for compliance.

These are policy directions, not quick fixes. The more Pakistan can link collection to documented activity, the less it will need to rely on blunt distinctions between filer and non-filer.

sections.title: Future Outlook
sections.body:
