  • Encouraging online tax filing through the FBR IRIS portal.
  • Promoting digital payment systems and electronic documentation.
  • Strengthening enforcement against tax evasion and underreporting.
  • Improving taxpayer services through online support and simplified procedures.
  • Increasing coordination between government institutions to identify non-filers and broaden the taxpayer base.

These policies are intended to create a fairer, more transparent, and more efficient tax system.

Tax reforms contribute to national development by increasing government revenue without relying excessively on borrowing. Higher tax collection enables greater investment in public services, transportation, education, healthcare, and social welfare programs. Digital tax reforms also encourage business formalization, improve investor confidence, and strengthen economic governance. As more businesses and individuals become part of the formal economy, Pakistan can build a more sustainable fiscal system and promote long-term economic growth.

sections.title: Challenges
sections.body:
Despite ongoing reforms, several challenges remain:

  • A large undocumented economy.
  • Low taxpayer awareness and voluntary compliance.
  • Complexity of tax regulations.
  • Limited digital access in some regions.
  • Resistance to formal registration among some businesses.

Addressing these issues will require continuous policy improvements, public awareness campaigns, investment in digital infrastructure, and stronger institutional capacity.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.body:
To further strengthen Pakistan's tax system, policymakers should:

  • Simplify tax laws and filing procedures.
  • Expand taxpayer education and awareness programs.
  • Improve digital infrastructure and cybersecurity.
  • Encourage voluntary compliance through incentives.
  • Strengthen enforcement against tax evasion while ensuring fairness.
  • Enhance transparency and accountability in tax administration.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The modernization of Pakistan's tax system through FBR reforms represents an important step toward improving fiscal stability and economic development. Expanding the tax base, adopting digital tax collection systems, and increasing tax compliance can help generate sustainable government revenue and support national development. Continued reforms, combined with public cooperation and effective implementation, will play a vital role in building a transparent, efficient, and equitable tax system for Pakistan.

publications.title: Fiscal Federalism in Pakistan
publications.author: Dr. Atiq ur Rehman
publications.description: An analysis of Pakistan's centralized resource management and a proposal for a structural overhaul towards devolved resource ownership.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Policy/Fiscal_Federalism_Pakistan_DrAtiqUrRehman/fiscal-federalism.png

sections.title: 摘要
sections.body:
Pakistan's prevailing model of centralized resource management has entrenched a cycle of interprovincial mistrust, fiscal dependency, and underutilization of natural wealth. This paper argues that the solution lies not in marginal reform but in a structural overhaul: the devolution of resource ownership, management, and revenue rights to federating units, coupled with a transparent, rules-based revenue-sharing framework with the federal government.

Drawing on the cases of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's hydroelectric resources and Azad Jammu & Kashmir's electricity generation capacity, the paper demonstrates that current pricing arrangements represent a systemic injustice that breeds resentment on all sides. It proposes an asymmetric fiscal federalism model in which provinces and territories manage their own resources at market rates, contribute an agreed share — approximately 40 percent — to the federal pool, and receive redistributive transfers based on objective criteria including poverty, underdevelopment, and population.

The paper further addresses the unique constitutional status of Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and argues that a de facto provincial status arrangement, pending final political resolution, is both legally tenable and practically necessary for this framework to succeed.

publications.title: Pakistan Diaspora Bonds
publications.author: Dr. Atiq ur Rehman, Associate Professor, University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir
publications.description: A proposal for sovereign instruments denominated in USD and purchased by overseas Pakistanis to address macroeconomic challenges.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Policy/PAKISTAN DIASPORA BONDS/PAKISTAN DIASPORA BONDS.png

sections.title: 执行摘要
sections.body:
Pakistan faces persistent macroeconomic challenges: volatile foreign exchange reserves, a heavy external debt servicing burden, and recurring reliance on IMF programs. With external debt and liabilities of approximately $138 billion as of late 2025 and liquid reserves near $22 billion, the country remains vulnerable to balance-of-payments shocks despite remittance inflows exceeding $38 billion in FY2025.

This paper proposes Pakistan Diaspora Bonds — sovereign instruments denominated in US dollars (or other major currencies) and purchased by overseas Pakistanis in foreign currency. Bonds are redeemable in Pakistani Rupees (PKR) at the prevailing interbank rate. Investors preferring foreign-currency redemption may do so, but receive only their original principal plus one-quarter of the prevailing Eurobond interest rate, making PKR redemption significantly more attractive. The government assumes exchange rate risk on PKR redemptions, but this creates only a domestic currency obligation — not a hard-currency liability — a structural advantage over Eurobonds and international Sukuk.

The scheme bundles time-phased social protections: life insurance at 5 times bond value; job displacement coverage at 3 times bond value; and family health insurance starting at 2 times bond value in Years 1–2, scaling to 5 times from Year 3, with a 25% co-payment and treatment restricted to empanelled hospitals throughout. Import duty exemptions on machinery and preferential business loans complete the incentive package.

The paper recommends forming an inter-ministerial task force within one month, drafting enabling legislation within six months, and launching a pilot issuance of $500 million to $1 billion in 2027.

publications.title: The Role of IMF Programs in Pakistan's Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Financial Lifelines with Strings Attached. A comprehensive look at the history and impact of IMF interventions in Pakistan.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/The Role of IMF Programs in Pakistan's Economy/The Role of IMF Programs in Pakistan's Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Pakistan's relationship with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is one of the most consequential and complex aspects of its economic history. Over the past several decades, Pakistan has entered into numerous IMF programs, making it one of the fund's most frequent clients among developing nations. These programs have provided critical financial support during balance of payments crises but have also imposed demanding conditions that profoundly affect the country's economic policy and the daily lives of its citizens.

sections.title: Why Pakistan Turns to the IMF
sections.body:
Pakistan's recurring need for IMF support reflects deep structural vulnerabilities in its economy. A persistent fiscal deficit—driven by inadequate tax revenues, high debt service costs, and substantial defense expenditures—requires consistent deficit financing. When external factors such as high oil prices, global economic slowdowns, or currency crises compound these internal weaknesses, Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves can deplete rapidly.

Once reserves fall below critical levels, the country struggles to finance essential imports—including fuel, food, and industrial inputs. Sovereign debt repayments come under threat, and international financial markets may become inaccessible or prohibitively expensive. In these circumstances, the IMF serves as the lender of last resort, providing emergency liquidity while helping to restore international confidence in Pakistan's economic management.

sections.title: What IMF Programs Involve
sections.body:
IMF support comes through various facilities—most commonly the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) for Pakistan—which provide access to foreign exchange in tranches, released upon successful completion of program reviews. Each review assesses whether Pakistan has met specific quantitative targets (such as fiscal deficit limits, reserve levels, and monetary policy benchmarks) and structural benchmarks (such as reforms to tax administration, state-owned enterprises, and energy pricing).

The conditionalities typically include measures to reduce the fiscal deficit through a combination of revenue enhancement and expenditure reduction, elimination or reduction of subsidies on energy and other commodities, exchange rate adjustment to eliminate overvaluation, monetary tightening to control inflation, and structural reforms to improve governance and reduce economic distortions.

sections.title: The Impact on Ordinary Pakistanis
sections.body:
IMF conditionalities, while economically rational from a stabilization perspective, often impose significant hardship on Pakistan's population, particularly its most vulnerable members. Subsidy cuts translate directly into higher prices for electricity, gas, and petroleum products—commodities essential to daily life. When energy subsidies are eliminated, electricity bills can increase dramatically, straining household budgets already stretched by high food prices.

Tax reforms, particularly the broadening of the sales tax base and increases in tax rates, raise the cost of goods and services. Fiscal consolidation measures often constrain public spending on social services, health, and education—reducing the quality and availability of services that lower-income households disproportionately depend upon.

The resulting economic slowdown and rising unemployment are significant human costs of adjustment programs. Workers in industries affected by higher energy costs or reduced government spending face job losses and wage stagnation.

sections.title: The Conditionality Debate
sections.body:
The appropriateness and effectiveness of IMF conditionalities in Pakistan's context remains a subject of significant debate among economists and policymakers. Critics argue that the fund's standard prescriptions—fiscal austerity, subsidy elimination, and monetary tightening—are too harsh in their immediate impact and fail to account for Pakistan's specific developmental needs and social vulnerabilities.

Proponents counter that without structural reforms, Pakistan would remain trapped in a cycle of crises requiring ever-larger bailouts. The conditionalities, while painful, are intended to create conditions for sustainable growth by eliminating market distortions, improving fiscal sustainability, and enhancing the competitiveness of the economy.

The reality appears to lie somewhere between these positions. While structural reforms are genuinely necessary, the speed and sequencing of their implementation, and the adequacy of accompanying social protection measures, significantly affect their impact on the population.

sections.title: Breaking the Cycle
sections.body: Pakistan's most fundamental challenge is to reduce its dependence on repeated IMF bailouts by addressing the underlying structural causes of its recurring crises. This requires a genuine expansion of the tax base to include previously exempt sectors such as real estate, retail, and agriculture; reducing the size and improving the efficiency of the public sector; developing export capacity to generate sustainable foreign exchange earnings; and building broad political consensus for sustained reform rather than reverting to populist policies between crises.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: IMF programs represent a critical but imperfect response to Pakistan's recurring economic crises. They provide essential financial breathing room and help catalyze reforms that might otherwise be politically impossible. However, their conditionalities impose real costs on the Pakistani population, particularly those who can least afford it. The ultimate goal must be to put Pakistan on a path of sufficient stability and growth that recurring IMF programs become unnecessary—a goal that requires sustained political commitment to difficult but essential structural reforms.

publications.title: The Rise of Digital Economies and Pakistan's Position
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Bridging the Gap Between Opportunity and Reality. How digital transformation is reshaping global trade and Pakistan's role.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/The Rise of Digital Economies and Pakistan's Position/The Rise of Digital Economies and Pakistan's Position.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The global economy is undergoing a profound digital transformation. From e-commerce and digital payments to artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and the platform economy, digital technologies are reshaping industries, creating new forms of value, and fundamentally altering the nature of work and trade. For Pakistan, this transformation presents a complex mix of opportunities to accelerate development and risks of being left further behind if adaptation is inadequate and too slow.

sections.title: The Scale of Digital Economic Opportunity
sections.body:
Pakistan's demographic profile creates significant potential for digital economic participation. With a median age below 25 and a rapidly growing population, the country has a large and growing pool of young people who are inherently more comfortable with digital technologies. Mobile phone penetration has expanded rapidly, creating the foundation for digital service delivery even in areas without traditional banking or physical commercial infrastructure.

The global freelancing economy has already created meaningful opportunities for skilled Pakistani workers in software development, graphic design, content creation, and digital marketing. Pakistan has emerged as one of the world's top countries by number of registered freelancers on global platforms, earning hundreds of millions of dollars annually in foreign exchange while working from Pakistani cities and towns.

sections.title: The IT Export Opportunity
sections.body:
Pakistan's IT and IT-enabled services sector has shown impressive growth, with exports growing from under a billion dollars annually to approaching three billion dollars in recent years. Software development, business process outsourcing, and digital services represent a potentially transformative opportunity for Pakistan to diversify its export base beyond traditional sectors like textiles.

Comparison with India's IT industry—which has grown to represent hundreds of billions of dollars in annual export earnings and supports millions of high-quality jobs—illustrates both the potential and the distance Pakistan has to travel. Realizing this potential requires sustained investment in technology education, supportive regulatory frameworks, reliable digital infrastructure, and an enabling business environment for tech startups and established IT firms alike.

sections.title: Digital Financial Inclusion
sections.body:
A large proportion of Pakistan's population remains excluded from formal financial services. Digital financial technologies—mobile wallets, digital payments, branchless banking—offer a pathway to include previously excluded populations in the formal economy, enabling them to save, receive payments, access credit, and build financial histories.

Initiatives like Raast—Pakistan's instant payment system—and the rapid growth of digital wallets have begun to accelerate financial inclusion. The Roshan Digital Account has successfully attracted overseas Pakistanis to open accounts and invest in Pakistan through digital channels. These developments, if sustained, could significantly expand the productive capacity of the economy by bringing more people and transactions into the formal financial system.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Structural Challenges
sections.body:
Despite promising developments, Pakistan faces significant structural challenges to digital economic participation. Internet penetration, while growing, remains incomplete—particularly in rural areas and among women, who face social and economic barriers to digital access. Connection quality and reliability are often inadequate for the demands of knowledge-intensive digital work.

Electricity reliability remains a fundamental constraint—frequent load-shedding that could disable productive digital work represents a particularly damaging problem for digital economy development. Regulatory frameworks for the digital economy are still developing, with some areas of policy creating uncertainty for businesses and investors.

The education system's output in terms of both the quantity and quality of technically trained graduates needs significant enhancement to support rapid digital sector growth. Bridging the gap between the skills demanded by global digital markets and those produced by Pakistan's education and training systems requires sustained investment and institutional reform.

sections.title: The Risk of Widening Divides
sections.body:
Without deliberate intervention, digital economic growth risks widening inequalities within Pakistan. The benefits of digital transformation naturally concentrate in urban areas, among the educated, and among those with reliable digital access. If rural communities, women, and low-education workers are excluded from digital economic opportunities, the digital transformation could reinforce and deepen existing social and economic divides.

Globally, as artificial intelligence accelerates automation, some traditional employment categories—including in textile production and basic services—may face technological displacement. Pakistan's large low-skilled workforce could face increased economic insecurity if this transition occurs without adequate preparation and social support systems.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The rise of digital economies presents Pakistan with a genuine opportunity to accelerate development, diversify exports, and include previously marginalized populations in productive economic activity. Realizing this potential requires determined policy action: investing in digital infrastructure, expanding technology education, creating enabling regulatory environments, and ensuring that digital opportunities are accessible across gender, geographic, and socioeconomic lines. The gap between Pakistan's digital potential and its current position can be closed—but it requires strategic commitment at the highest levels of government, sustained over years rather than election cycles.

publications.title: Remittances and Overseas Pakistani Workers in a Slowing Global Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: A Lifeline Under Pressure. Assessing the trends in remittance inflows as global growth slows.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Remittances and Overseas Pakistani Workers in a Slowing Global Economy/Remittances and Overseas Pakistani Workers in a Slowing Global Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Remittances—the money sent home by Pakistanis working abroad—constituute one of the most important and reliable sources of foreign exchange for Pakistan's economy. In many years, remittance inflows have exceeded the total value of export earnings from any single sector, including textiles, making them a critical component of the country's balance of payments. However, this lifeline is sensitive to economic conditions in host countries, particularly in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region where a large proportion of overseas Pakistanis work.

sections.title: The Scale of Pakistan's Diaspora Economy
sections.body:
Pakistan has one of the world's largest overseas labor forces, with estimates suggesting eight to nine million Pakistanis work abroad. The Gulf states—Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman—host the largest concentration, primarily in construction, services, and labor-intensive sectors. Significant Pakistani communities also exist in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, and Europe.

In recent years, remittances to Pakistan have reached $25-30 billion annually, making the country one of the world's top remittance-receiving nations. These flows directly support millions of families across Pakistan, fund housing construction, finance education and healthcare, and contribute significantly to domestic consumption.

sections.title: The Gulf Economy's Sensitivity to Oil Prices
sections.body:
The GCC economies that employ the largest numbers of Pakistani workers are heavily dependent on oil revenues. When global oil prices fall sharply—as they did in 2014-16 and briefly in 2020—Gulf economies contract, government revenues decline, and development projects slow or halt. The construction sector, which employs large numbers of Pakistani workers, is particularly sensitive to these slowdowns.

During periods of Gulf economic stress, job creation slows, existing workers may face contract terminations or non-renewal, and some return to Pakistan without the expected earnings. Lower oil prices thus create a double negative for Pakistan: the country benefits from lower import costs but suffers from reduced remittance inflows, and the net effect can be negative given the large number of workers in the Gulf.

sections.title: Impact of Global Economic Slowdowns
sections.body:
Beyond the Gulf, economic slowdowns in developed countries where significant Pakistani diaspora communities reside—particularly the UK and the US—also reduce remittance flows. During recessions, overseas Pakistanis face higher unemployment risk, lower wage growth, and reduced discretionary income available to send home. The pandemic's economic shock simultaneously affected jobs across multiple host countries, creating a significant risk to remittance flows (though in practice, remittances proved more resilient than feared in 2020-21).

The long-term demographic and economic evolution of host countries also matters. As Gulf economies seek to reduce their labor import dependency and develop more technology-intensive economies, the demand for lower-skilled Pakistani labor could decline structurally over time.

sections.title: Digital Channels and Formal Remittances
sections.body:
A significant proportion of remittances historically flowed through informal channels—the hawala system—rather than formal banking and money transfer operators. While this met the needs of senders and receivers, it meant these flows were not captured in official statistics and did not benefit the formal financial system or foreign exchange reserves.

Government initiatives to shift remittances to formal channels—including the Roshan Digital Account scheme—have had some success in increasing the documented flow of remittances through official channels. Digital money transfer services have also made formal remittance channels more competitive in terms of cost and convenience, potentially drawing more flows into the formal system.

sections.title: Protecting the Remittance Lifeline
sections.body:
Protecting and growing remittance flows requires attention to several dimensions. Diplomacy to protect the rights and working conditions of Pakistani workers abroad—ensuring their contracts are honored and their access to legal recourse is maintained—is essential for worker welfare and continued employment.

Domestically, creating an environment where remittances are channeled into productive investment rather than solely consumption would multiply their economic impact. Improving financial inclusion so that recipient families can access banking services, and developing investment products that make it attractive for overseas Pakistanis to invest remittances in Pakistan's economy, would enhance the developmental impact of these flows.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Remittances represent an indispensable economic lifeline for Pakistan—supporting millions of families and contributing significantly to the country's foreign exchange earnings. However, this lifeline is not unconditional: it depends on continued employment opportunities for Pakistani workers abroad and favorable economic conditions in host countries. As global economic headwinds increase and Gulf economies evolve, Pakistan must both protect existing remittance flows and develop the domestic economic opportunities that would reduce the country's dependence on labor export as a primary development strategy.

publications.title: Oil Prices and Pakistan's Economic Stability
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: The Double-Edged Impact of Global Energy Markets. Exploring the correlation between international oil price volatility and Pakistan's stability.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Oil Prices and Pakistan's Economic Stability/Oil Prices and Pakistan's Economic Stability.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Few factors influence Pakistan's economy as directly and dramatically as global oil prices. As a country that imports the vast majority of its petroleum requirements, Pakistan is acutely sensitive to the fluctuations in crude oil markets driven by the decisions of OPEC nations, geopolitical events, and global demand dynamics. Understanding this relationship illuminates much of Pakistan's recurring economic challenges and the difficulty of achieving sustained stability.

sections.title: Pakistan's Oil Import Dependency
sections.body:
Pakistan's domestic oil production covers only a small fraction of its energy needs. The country relies heavily on imported crude oil and petroleum products to fuel its transportation sector, power its industries, and run its thermal power plants. In recent years, petroleum imports have consistently constituted one of the largest components of Pakistan's import bill, frequently accounting for a quarter to a third of total import expenditure.

This structural dependency means that when global oil prices rise, Pakistan's import bill surges correspondingly, straining its balance of payments position and depleting foreign exchange reserves. The country has limited ability to reduce oil consumption quickly due to the lack of adequate alternative energy infrastructure.

sections.title: OPEC Decisions and Their Ripple Effects
sections.body:
The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its extended alliance, OPEC+, wield enormous influence over global oil prices through production quotas. When these oil-producing nations decide to cut production—as they have done repeatedly in recent years—global supply tightens and prices rise. Pakistan has no seat at the OPEC table and no ability to influence these decisions, yet their consequences are immediately felt by Pakistani consumers and businesses.

Beyond OPEC decisions, geopolitical events such as conflicts in oil-producing regions, sanctions on major exporters, and disruptions to shipping routes can cause sudden and severe price spikes. Pakistan's economy is exposed to all of these external shocks with limited hedging mechanisms or strategic reserves to cushion the impact.

sections.title: Cascading Economic Effects
sections.body:
The economic effects of oil price increases in Pakistan cascade through multiple channels. Most directly, higher oil prices inflate the cost of transportation, affecting the price of virtually every good and service in the economy. Freight costs for goods transported across the country rise, adding to inflationary pressures already built up through other channels.

The energy sector feels the impact acutely. Pakistan's thermal power plants, which generate a substantial portion of electricity, face higher fuel costs. These costs are eventually passed on to consumers through higher electricity tariffs, affecting household budgets and industrial competitiveness alike. Energy-intensive industries—from cement to fertilizer production—see their cost structures worsen, reducing their ability to compete in export markets.

The trade deficit widens as the import bill grows faster than export revenues. This puts pressure on foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate, which in turn amplifies inflationary pressures as the weaker rupee makes all imports more expensive, creating a vicious economic cycle.

sections.title: The Energy Crisis Dimension
sections.body:
High oil prices also interact with Pakistan's chronic energy crisis. When global LNG prices spike—as they did dramatically following the Russia-Ukraine conflict—Pakistan struggles to secure adequate fuel supplies for its power plants. The result is extended load-shedding that cripples industrial production, disrupts businesses and households, and imposes enormous economic costs.

The inability to afford sufficient energy imports during price spikes has repeatedly pushed Pakistan's industrial sector into crisis, with factories shutting down or operating at reduced capacity. This undermines employment, export earnings, and economic growth—creating a multiplier effect that extends far beyond the direct cost of higher fuel prices.

sections.title: Policy Options and Structural Solutions
sections.body:
Pakistan's approach to managing oil price volatility has historically relied on price subsidies, which provide short-term relief but are fiscally unsustainable. A more durable solution requires accelerating the transition to domestic renewable energy sources—solar, wind, and hydropower—which would reduce dependence on expensive imported fuels.

Improving energy efficiency across transportation, industry, and buildings would reduce the volume of oil required. Developing strategic petroleum reserves would provide a buffer during price spikes. These measures require significant upfront investment but would substantially reduce Pakistan's vulnerability to global oil market volatility over the medium term.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Oil prices represent one of the most powerful external forces shaping Pakistan's economic trajectory. The country's structural dependency on imported petroleum makes it acutely vulnerable to global market fluctuations driven by OPEC decisions, geopolitical developments, and supply-demand dynamics beyond its control. Building economic stability in this context requires a fundamental transformation of Pakistan's energy sector—reducing fossil fuel dependence, developing domestic renewable capacity, and improving efficiency across the economy.

publications.title: Interest Rate Hikes by Central Banks and Pakistan's Debt Burden
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: The Cost of Global Monetary Tightening. Assessing the ripple effect of global interest rate fluctuations on Pakistan's debt.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Interest Rate Hikes by Central Banks and Pakistan's Debt Burden/Interest Rate Hikes by Central Banks and Pakistan's Debt Burden.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: When the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates, the effects are felt far beyond American shores. For developing countries like Pakistan—already burdened with substantial external debt—the global monetary tightening cycle initiated by major central banks represents a serious threat to economic stability. Understanding this relationship is crucial for policymakers, businesses, and citizens trying to navigate Pakistan's complex economic landscape.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Global Rate Hikes
sections.body:
Central banks in advanced economies—particularly the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of England—raise interest rates primarily to combat domestic inflation. By making borrowing more expensive, they aim to reduce consumer spending and business investment, thereby cooling inflationary pressures.

However, these rate hikes have profound global implications. When US interest rates rise, dollar-denominated assets become more attractive to global investors. Capital flows out of emerging markets and into the US, seeking higher and safer returns. This capital flight reduces the supply of foreign exchange in countries like Pakistan, putting downward pressure on their currencies.

sections.title: Pakistan's External Debt Landscape
sections.body:
Pakistan carries a substantial external debt burden, a significant portion of which is denominated in US dollars or linked to variable interest rates. As of recent years, Pakistan's total public debt has exceeded 70% of GDP, with external debt obligations requiring billions of dollars in annual repayments.

When global interest rates rise, two mechanisms worsen Pakistan's debt situation. First, the cost of new borrowing increases—whether from international capital markets, bilateral creditors, or multilateral institutions. Any new loans taken to refinance existing debt or fund development projects become significantly more expensive.

Second, for debt linked to variable rates (such as loans tied to LIBOR or its successor SOFR), existing obligations automatically become more costly. Pakistan must allocate more of its scarce foreign exchange reserves to service these rising debt costs, leaving less for essential imports or development spending.

sections.title: Currency Depreciation: A Compounding Effect
sections.body:
Rising global interest rates trigger currency depreciation in Pakistan through two channels. As capital flows toward higher-yielding dollar assets, demand for the Pakistani rupee falls while demand for dollars rises. This pushes the rupee's value down against the dollar.

A weaker rupee makes every dollar of external debt more expensive in rupee terms. If the rupee depreciates by 20%, the rupee cost of a dollar-denominated loan repayment increases by the same proportion. This effectively magnifies Pakistan's debt burden without any new borrowing—simply through currency dynamics.

Furthermore, currency depreciation fuels domestic inflation by raising the cost of imports, creating a self-reinforcing cycle: inflation prompts further monetary tightening globally, which causes further capital outflows and rupee depreciation, which drives more domestic inflation.

sections.title: IMF Conditionalities and Fiscal Space
sections.body:
Pakistan's recourse to IMF support during debt crises typically comes with conditionalities that further constrain its policy options. Interest rate hikes demanded by the IMF to control domestic inflation and attract foreign investment conflict with the need for affordable credit for businesses and households. The resulting economic slowdown reduces tax revenues precisely when the government needs additional resources to service its debt.

This tension between debt service obligations, IMF conditionalities, and the need for economic growth represents one of Pakistan's most difficult policy challenges. The country finds itself in a situation where external monetary dynamics beyond its control significantly constrain its domestic policy choices.

sections.title: Pathways to Resilience
sections.body:
Building resilience against global interest rate fluctuations requires Pakistan to pursue several long-term strategies. Reducing dependence on external borrowing through improving domestic revenue mobilization is essential. Expanding the tax base, improving collection efficiency, and reducing leakages would give Pakistan greater fiscal independence.

Diversifying the debt portfolio to include more concessional loans from multilateral sources, exploring local currency financing options, and building adequate foreign exchange reserves are also critical. Additionally, structural reforms that enhance export competitiveness would generate the dollar inflows needed to reduce dependence on debt financing.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Pakistan's debt burden is acutely sensitive to global interest rate dynamics. When major central banks tighten monetary policy, the resulting capital outflows, currency depreciation, and higher borrowing costs create a perfect storm for debt-laden developing economies. For Pakistan, the path forward requires both immediate crisis management and sustained structural reforms to reduce vulnerability to these external monetary shocks that originate in Washington, Frankfurt, and London but are painfully felt in Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad.

publications.title: Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Vulnerability Exposed in an Interconnected World. Analyzing how bottlenecks in global logistics are affecting Pakistan's industries.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries/Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Pakistan's Industries.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of global supply chains with dramatic clarity. What had previously been an abstract concern for logistics specialists became a visceral reality for manufacturers, retailers, and consumers worldwide. For Pakistan, whose industrial sector—particularly textiles and manufacturing—is deeply integrated into global supply networks, supply chain disruptions represent a significant and recurring threat to economic activity, employment, and export earnings.

sections.title: How Global Supply Chains Work And Fail
sections.body:
Modern manufacturing relies on complex, geographically dispersed supply chains. A textile manufacturer in Pakistan may use cotton from local farms, dyes from China, synthetic fibers from petrochemical producers, specialized machinery from Germany, and finishing chemicals from Europe. This global sourcing strategy optimizes costs but creates multiple points of vulnerability—any disruption anywhere in the chain can halt production.

When the pandemic simultaneously disrupted production at multiple nodes of these chains—as factories closed, workers fell ill, ports became congested, and transport capacity collapsed—the cascading effects spread rapidly across the global economy. Even after immediate production disruptions eased, shipping bottlenecks, container shortages, and logistics backlogs kept supply chains dysfunctional for months.

sections.title: Pakistan's Textile Sector: The Most Exposed
sections.body:
Pakistan's textile sector—which accounts for approximately 60% of the country's export earnings and employs millions—is particularly vulnerable to global supply chain disruptions. While Pakistan produces significant quantities of cotton domestically, the sector depends on imports for man-made fibers, specialized dyes, chemicals, and manufacturing equipment.

During the pandemic-era disruptions, Pakistani textile exporters faced a double challenge. On the supply side, delays and cost increases in imported inputs raised production costs and created uncertainty about delivery timelines. On the demand side, order cancellations by international buyers—particularly in the initial phase of the pandemic when global retail collapsed—left factories with unsold inventory and idle production capacity.

Freight rate increases during the supply chain crisis were dramatic—container shipping rates increased by factors of five to ten in some trade lanes—significantly eroding the competitiveness of Pakistan's exports by raising the landed cost of goods in destination markets.

sections.title: Manufacturing Beyond Textiles
sections.body:
While textiles face the most acute exposure, other manufacturing sectors are also vulnerable. Pakistan's pharmaceutical industry depends on active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and other raw materials largely sourced from China and India. When disruptions in these source countries constrained supply, Pakistan's domestic medicine production faced shortages of essential inputs.

The automotive and electronics assembly sectors, though smaller, depend on imported components and are completely halted when supply chain disruptions prevent the arrival of critical parts. Even Pakistan's construction sector is not immune—import dependencies for steel, specialized equipment, and certain building materials mean that global supply disruptions affect domestic development projects.

sections.title: Structural Vulnerabilities and Opportunities
sections.body:
The supply chain disruptions of the pandemic era revealed Pakistan's structural vulnerability to external shocks while simultaneously creating potential opportunities. As global companies sought to diversify their supply chains away from excessive dependence on single-country sources—particularly China—Pakistan had an opportunity to attract relocated or diversified production capacity.

However, capturing this opportunity required Pakistan to address longstanding competitive weaknesses: high energy costs, unreliable electricity supply, burdensome regulatory frameworks, inadequate logistics infrastructure, and skill gaps in the workforce. The countries that successfully attracted supply chain relocation—Vietnam, Bangladesh, and others—had developed competitive advantages in these areas over years of sustained policy attention.

sections.title: Building Supply Chain Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's approach to building supply chain resilience must operate on multiple levels. At the firm level, businesses can develop more diverse supplier relationships, maintain larger buffer inventories of critical inputs, and invest in process flexibility. At the sector level, industry associations can coordinate to develop alternative sourcing strategies and advocate for policy support.

At the national level, policies that develop domestic capabilities in key input industries reduce import dependence. Improving logistics infrastructure—ports, roads, warehousing, and digital trade facilitation—reduces the impact of external disruptions on domestic production. Trade agreements that provide alternative market access and supply sources enhance resilience.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Global supply chain disruptions have revealed the vulnerability embedded in Pakistan's industrial integration into global networks. The country's textile and manufacturing sectors, while benefiting enormously from global integration in normal times, face severe stress when those networks are disrupted by pandemics, geopolitical conflicts, or natural disasters. Building resilience requires both firm-level adaptations and national policy reforms that address structural weaknesses—ensuring that Pakistan can maintain production and protect livelihoods even when global supply networks are under strain.

publications.title: Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Rising Costs, Shrinking Wallets. An analysis of how global inflationary pressures translate into a domestic crisis in Pakistan.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The world economy is experiencing a significant inflationary wave, with major economies like the United States and the European Union grappling with rising prices across virtually every sector. This global phenomenon is not confined to the borders of advanced economies—it ripples outward, touching developing nations like Pakistan with particularly harsh consequences. For a country already struggling with fiscal imbalances and a fragile economic structure, external inflationary pressures can quickly translate into a crisis of daily survival for millions of citizens.

sections.title: How Global Inflation Reaches Pakistan
sections.body:
Pakistan is a net importer of several essential commodities, including petroleum products, edible oils, industrial raw materials, and machinery. When inflation rises in major economies, the cost of producing and exporting these goods increases. This means Pakistan pays more for the same volume of imports, effectively importing inflation from abroad.

Additionally, the US Dollar's dominant role in global trade means that when the dollar strengthens—as it often does during inflationary periods driven by monetary tightening—Pakistan's rupee buys less in the international market. The result is a compounding effect: higher global prices combined with a weaker domestic currency create a double burden on the Pakistani economy.

sections.title: Impact on Fuel, Food, and Raw Materials
sections.body:
Three sectors feel the impact most acutely. First, fuel: Pakistan is heavily dependent on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). As global energy prices surge—driven by geopolitical tensions, OPEC decisions, and post-pandemic demand rebounds—Pakistan's energy import bill skyrockets. This makes electricity generation, transportation, and industrial production more expensive, cascading into higher prices across the entire economy.

Second, food prices: global food inflation, partly driven by supply chain disruptions, climate events, and conflict zones, raises the cost of imported edible oils, wheat, and pulses. For a country where food constitutes a large portion of household budgets, this directly diminishes the purchasing power of ordinary Pakistanis.

Third, raw materials: industries ranging from textiles to chemicals depend on imported inputs. When these become expensive, production costs rise, leading to either higher prices for consumers or reduced output—neither of which is desirable.

sections.title: The Human Cost
sections.body: The most direct consequence of imported inflation is felt by low- and middle-income households. As prices of everyday essentials—flour, cooking oil, electricity, fuel—climb relentlessly, families find themselves spending a larger fraction of their income just to maintain basic living standards. Savings shrink, debt increases, and poverty rates rise. Pakistan's already stretched social safety nets come under enormous pressure, often proving inadequate to cushion the most vulnerable segments of society.

sections.title: Policy Responses and Their Limitations
sections.body:
The Pakistani government and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) have attempted to manage inflationary pressures through a combination of monetary tightening, subsidies, and import controls. Raising interest rates, for example, can reduce domestic demand and cool inflation but also stifles economic growth and raises the cost of borrowing for businesses and individuals alike.

Subsidies on fuel and food can provide short-term relief but are fiscally unsustainable, especially for a country with limited revenue and a heavy debt burden. Import restrictions may protect foreign exchange reserves in the short run but can lead to shortages and black markets.

Ultimately, Pakistan's capacity to insulate itself from global inflationary waves is constrained by structural vulnerabilities: a narrow export base, low foreign exchange reserves, high import dependence, and limited fiscal space. Addressing these structural issues is essential for building resilience against future inflationary shocks.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The global inflation wave is a sobering reminder of how interconnected today's economies are. For Pakistan, rising international prices translate directly into hardship for its citizens, straining household budgets and government finances alike. While short-term policy measures can offer some relief, the deeper solution lies in structural reforms that reduce import dependence, boost exports, enhance productivity, and build fiscal buffers. Until such reforms take root, Pakistan will remain acutely vulnerable to the economic tides that originate far beyond its borders.

publications.title: Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: How the World's Reserve Currency Shapes Pakistan's Economy. Investigating the impact of a strong US Dollar on the Pakistani Rupee.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The US dollar's role as the world's dominant reserve currency and primary medium of international trade creates a structural asymmetry in the global economy. Countries that earn and hold reserves in dollars benefit from its stability and universal acceptance. Countries like Pakistan that must buy dollars to pay for essential imports and service dollar-denominated debt face a fundamental vulnerability: their economic well-being is significantly influenced by the value of a currency they do not control and a monetary policy set for American domestic conditions.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Rupee Depreciation
sections.body:
The Pakistani rupee's value is determined in foreign exchange markets by the supply and demand for rupees relative to other currencies, particularly the dollar. Several factors create persistent downward pressure on the rupee.

Pakistan's structural trade deficit—importing significantly more than it exports—means that the economy continuously demands more dollars than it earns from exports. This excess demand for dollars creates inherent depreciation pressure. When this deficit is not offset by sufficient inflows of foreign investment, remittances, or borrowing, reserves deplete and the rupee falls.

When the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates, the dollar strengthens globally as international capital flows toward higher-yielding dollar assets. This dollar appreciation is simultaneously rupee depreciation—the mirror image of dollar strength. Thus, American monetary policy decisions intended to address US domestic inflation directly affect Pakistan's exchange rate.

sections.title: The Import Cost Amplification
sections.body:
Currency depreciation creates an immediate and painful amplification of import costs. If Pakistan imports a barrel of oil at $80, and the rupee has depreciated by 20% over a year, the rupee cost of that same barrel has increased by 20%—even if the dollar price of oil remained unchanged.

This mechanism means that Pakistan effectively faces a double burden during periods of global stress: international commodity prices often rise at the same time that the rupee falls, as both are driven by dollar strengthening and global risk aversion. The combination of higher dollar prices and a weaker rupee can dramatically increase the rupee cost of essential imports within a short period, generating intense inflationary pressure.

sections.title: Impact on Businesses and Consumers
sections.body:
The business community faces multiple challenges from currency depreciation. Importers see their costs rise immediately when the rupee depreciates. Manufacturers who use imported raw materials face rising input costs, which they must either absorb—reducing profit margins—or pass on to consumers, contributing to inflation.

Exporters benefit from rupee depreciation in theory, as their goods become cheaper in international markets in dollar terms. However, if their production costs rise due to imported inputs and higher energy costs (themselves partly driven by import costs), the competitive gain is offset. The net benefit to exporters depends on their specific cost structure and the degree to which they can expand production at lower cost in dollar terms.

For consumers, currency depreciation is experienced as higher prices across virtually the entire basket of goods and services. From fuel prices at petrol stations to the cost of electronics, medicines, and processed foods—the depreciated rupee makes everything more expensive.

sections.title: The Political Economy of Exchange Rate Management
sections.body:
Managing the exchange rate involves difficult political choices. Artificially maintaining an overvalued exchange rate by intervening in currency markets to support the rupee can provide temporary relief from import cost increases but depletes foreign exchange reserves and creates distortions that ultimately require more painful correction.

Allowing market-determined exchange rate adjustments as required under IMF programs is often more economically rational but politically contentious given its immediate inflationary impact. Pakistani governments have historically alternated between periods of exchange rate suppression and sharp devaluations, each creating its own set of economic distortions and hardships.

sections.title: Reducing Dollar Vulnerability
sections.body:
Pakistan's long-term vulnerability to dollar dominance can be reduced through several strategies. Building export capacity across diverse sectors generates more dollar earnings domestically, reducing net import demand. Developing domestic production of currently imported goods reduces the dollar demand created by imports.

Diversifying trade and financing relationships—including increasing use of local currencies in bilateral trade with neighboring countries like China and the Gulf states—reduces, at the margin, the exclusive dominance of the dollar in Pakistan's international transactions. Building adequate foreign exchange reserves provides a buffer against short-term pressure without requiring immediate adjustment.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The dollar's dominance in global trade and finance creates a structural challenge for Pakistan that cannot be resolved through exchange rate policy alone. Currency depreciation is both a symptom of underlying economic imbalances and a cause of further inflation and financial stress. Addressing Pakistan's currency vulnerability requires the hard work of structural economic transformation—building exports, reducing import dependence, improving fiscal discipline, and creating the conditions for stable, growth-enabling investment flows.

publications.title: Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Living on the Front Lines of a Global Crisis. How international climate agreements are shaping Pakistan's economic landscape.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Pakistan stands at a painful paradox in the global climate crisis. Despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, the country ranks consistently among the world's most vulnerable nations to the physical impacts of climate change. Extreme heat waves, devastating floods, glacial lake outburst floods, drought, and crop failures are no longer theoretical future scenarios—they are lived realities that are already reshaping Pakistan's economy and threatening its development trajectory.

sections.title: The Physical Reality of Climate Impacts
sections.body:
Pakistan's geographical position makes it acutely sensitive to climate variability. The 2022 super-floods—described by scientists as made significantly more likely and severe by climate change—provide the starkest illustration. These floods inundated approximately one-third of the country's land mass, killed over 1,700 people, displaced millions, destroyed critical infrastructure, and caused economic losses estimated at over $30 billion.

Agricultural losses during the 2022 floods were catastrophic: millions of acres of crops destroyed, vast livestock herds lost, and irrigation infrastructure damaged. In a country where agriculture employs approximately 40% of the workforce and contributes around 20% of GDP, such losses have profound ripple effects throughout the economy. Reduced agricultural output drives food price inflation, reduces rural incomes, and increases food import requirements—all adding pressure to an already strained economy.

sections.title: Recurring Climate Shocks and Economic Stability
sections.body:
The 2022 floods were an extreme event but not an isolated one. Pakistan has experienced increasingly frequent and severe climate-related disruptions: intense heat waves that reduce agricultural productivity and worker output, irregular monsoons that affect crop planting and yields, glacial melting that threatens the long-term water security of the Indus Basin, and coastal erosion threatening populated areas in Sindh and Balochistan.

These recurring shocks create an environment of economic uncertainty that discourages investment, disrupts planning, and imposes continuous repair and recovery costs on a country with already limited fiscal resources. The cumulative economic cost of climate impacts—even without considering catastrophic events like the 2022 floods—represents a significant drag on Pakistan's development potential.

sections.title: International Climate Finance and Pakistan
sections.body:
The global discussion on climate finance has created both opportunities and frustrations for Pakistan. Developed countries have pledged billions in climate finance to help developing nations adapt to climate change and transition to cleaner energy—but the delivery of these commitments has been inconsistent and often falls short of pledged amounts.

Following the 2022 floods, Pakistan's advocacy for climate justice and loss-and-damage compensation drew international attention and contributed to the establishment of a Loss and Damage Fund at COP27. Accessing and effectively utilizing climate finance requires Pakistan to develop strong project pipelines, transparent financial management systems, and institutional capacity to negotiate with international climate funds.

sections.title: Global Climate Policies and Pakistan's Exports
sections.body:
Beyond direct physical impacts, global climate policies create important economic implications for Pakistan. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)—which imposes carbon costs on imports from countries without equivalent carbon pricing—threatens to raise the cost of Pakistani exports entering the EU market over time.

Pakistan's export-oriented industries, particularly textiles and leather, will face pressure to document and reduce their carbon footprints to maintain market access in climate-conscious importing countries. This creates both a compliance cost and an investment opportunity—firms that successfully transition to cleaner production processes may gain competitive advantages in premium export markets that reward sustainability credentials.

sections.title: Building Climate Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's national climate strategy must address both adaptation—reducing vulnerability to impacts that are already locked in—and mitigation—reducing emissions as part of the global effort to limit future warming. Adaptation priorities include flood protection infrastructure, drought-resistant crop varieties, efficient irrigation systems, early warning systems, and climate-resilient construction standards.

Mitigation involves transitioning Pakistan's energy sector toward renewables, improving energy efficiency, developing sustainable transportation, and protecting forests. Many of these investments have co-benefits for economic development—renewable energy reduces fuel import bills, efficient irrigation improves agricultural productivity, and forest protection supports rural livelihoods.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Climate change represents an existential economic threat for Pakistan—one that is already manifesting in devastating floods, disrupted agriculture, and increased reliance on international emergency assistance. Pakistan's experience challenges the international community to deliver meaningful climate finance and ambitious emission reductions. Domestically, building climate resilience requires sustained investment, institutional development, and policy coherence across economic sectors. The cost of inaction—measured in recurring disasters, agricultural decline, and development setbacks—far exceeds the investment required for adaptation and mitigation.

publications.title: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Promises, Progress, and Shifting Priorities. An analysis of CPEC's trajectory amidst shifting global economic dynamics.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) was launched with enormous ambition—a flagship project of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) that promised to transform Pakistan's infrastructure, energy sector, and economic connectivity while cementing a strategic partnership between the two neighboring nations. A decade into implementation, CPEC has delivered significant results in certain areas while facing challenges from Pakistan's economic difficulties, changing global dynamics, and shifts in China's own economic priorities.

sections.title: CPEC's Foundational Vision
sections.body:
At its core, CPEC envisions connecting China's landlocked western Xinjiang region to the Arabian Sea through Pakistan's Gwadar port, creating a shorter and more economical route for Chinese trade and energy imports from the Middle East and Africa. For Pakistan, the corridor was meant to address two critical bottlenecks: an acute energy shortage crippling industrial production and an inadequate transportation network limiting economic activity.

The $62 billion investment—though revised figures vary—was structured to deliver energy projects, road and rail upgrades, and special economic zones (SEZs) that would attract industrial investment and create employment. The vision was of a Pakistan transformed into a regional hub of trade and manufacturing.

sections.title: Progress and Achievements
sections.body:
CPEC has delivered tangible results in Pakistan's power sector. Numerous energy projects—coal, solar, and hydropower—have been completed or are operational, adding significant capacity to the national grid. This has reduced, though not eliminated, Pakistan's chronic electricity shortages that had long suppressed industrial output.

Infrastructure investments have improved road connectivity in various corridors, and Gwadar port has seen significant development. These investments have created employment during construction and improved logistics in certain regions. For Pakistan, attracting such large-scale foreign investment at concessional terms was an achievement in itself given the country's challenging business environment.

sections.title: Challenges and Controversies
sections.body:
CPEC has also generated significant controversy and faces serious challenges. Critics have raised concerns about the transparency of contracts, the terms of financing, and the extent to which Pakistani businesses benefit from CPEC projects—noting that many contracts were awarded to Chinese firms with limited local participation.

The debt obligations associated with CPEC projects—including principal repayments and repatriated profits from independent power producers—have contributed to Pakistan's external financial pressures. The promised industrial cooperation through SEZs has been slower to materialize than anticipated, limiting the employment generation and technology transfer that were central to CPEC's developmental promises.

Geopolitical tensions in the region, security challenges—particularly in Balochistan, and inconsistent policy support from successive Pakistani governments have all slowed implementation.

sections.title: China's Changing Economic Priorities
sections.body:
China's own economic situation is evolving in ways that affect CPEC's trajectory. China's growth has moderated from its earlier double-digit rates, and the country is navigating significant internal economic transitions. The BRI overall has faced scrutiny over debt sustainability concerns, and China has become more selective and cautious in its overseas infrastructure investments.

This shift in Chinese priorities, combined with Pakistan's financial difficulties limiting its ability to fulfill obligations and attract complementary investments, means that CPEC's second phase focusing on industrial development has progressed more slowly than initially envisioned. Both countries need to recalibrate expectations and focus on ensuring that existing investments deliver their intended benefits before committing to ambitious new phases.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.body:
For CPEC to fulfill its transformative potential, several conditions are necessary. Pakistan must improve its business environment through regulatory reforms, consistent policy frameworks, and enhanced security—making SEZs genuinely attractive to both Chinese and international investors. Renegotiating the terms of existing energy agreements to reduce their fiscal burden on Pakistan would improve the corridor's overall economic sustainability.

Diversifying CPEC's scope to include more agriculture, technology, and services cooperation alongside physical infrastructure would better leverage Pakistan's comparative advantages. Greater transparency in project contracts and more meaningful participation of Pakistani firms would also address legitimate concerns about the distribution of benefits.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: CPEC remains a vital component of Pakistan's development strategy and a cornerstone of its strategic relationship with China. Despite falling short of its most ambitious initial projections, the corridor has delivered real infrastructure improvements and energy capacity. In a changing global economy where great power competition intensifies and China recalibrates its overseas investments, Pakistan must be a proactive and strategic partner—ensuring that CPEC delivers lasting economic benefits rather than merely creating debt obligations and foreign-dominated enclaves.

publications.title: Introduction to Monetary Economics
publications.author: Atiq Ur Rehman, Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Monetary Economics, 1st Edition. This book will be of interest to teachers and students of monetary economics, money and banking, macroeconomics and monetary policy.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Books/cover-image.png

sections.title: Major Features of this Edition
sections.body:
• Moderated Stylized facts on money demand and supply, and the relationships between monetary policy, inflation, output and unemployment in the economy.
  • Theories on money demand and supply, including precautionary and buffer stock models, and monetary aggregation.
  • Competing macroeconomic models of the Classical and Keynesian paradigms, along with a discussion of their validity and consistency with the stylized facts.
  • Excellent pedagogical features such as introductions, key concepts, end-of-chapter summaries, and review and discussion questions.

sections.title: About the Authors
sections.body:
Dr. Atiq ur Rehman is Associate Professor of Economics at University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, UAJK and has taught monetary economics and macroeconomics for over 15 years.

Dr. Shakeel Shahzad is Assistant Professor of Economics at Bahria University, Islamabad and has taught monetary economics, macroeconomics, and econometrics for over 10 years.

publications.title: Role of Remittance’s in Pakistan Economy; Analysis of the current status and guideline for Reforms
publications.author: Attiya Y. Javid 教授/博士
publications.description: 提交给高等教育委员会的最终报告。
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Reports/HEC final Report (Prof. Dr. Attiya Y. Javid - 21052020) (1)/Cover-image.png

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body:
Remittances for a very respectable size in the economy of Pakistan, and they form about 8.8% of GDP. These remittances play extremely important in management of Pakistan economy, mainly contributing to the management of current account balance. For a long period over the history, Pakistan is facing large trade deficit and the remittances are used to bring the current account deficit at balance. However, when remittances reach the country through formal channels, the bank keep the foreign currency with them and pay rupee in exchange of it. Thus about Rs. 3.3 trillion come into the pockets of recipients. The earlier studies on remittances show that the marginal propensity to save for the remitters is much higher compared to the overall propensity to save. Supposing marginal propensity to save to be only 20%, the amount of saving should be sufficient to finance millions of jobs. But no job related activities are observable.

The first question arises that how remittances contribute to the economy? A model was estimated using WALS approach which show that the huge surge in remittances didn’t effect the pace of growth of economy.

The second question that arises is; what is happening to the remittances that they don’t contribute to economy. Extensive Survey was carried out in selected cities of all four provinces, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad Capital territory and Gilgit Baltistan to find the answer to this question. The findings reveal that largest share of the investable part of remittances goes into real estate, especially sale and purchase of plots which is extremely capital intensive business and one doesn’t contribute to the employment generation and any other economic benefit.

The next important question was to recommend the measures for enhancing the flow of remittances through formal channels and to recommend measures for welfare of remittances. We propose that in order to increase the formal inflow, SBP should subsidize the formal inflow. This subsidy would be proportional to size of remittances and would not be directly encashable. Half of this subsidy is deposited to the premium for health and life insurance of the remitter and his/her family and remaining half of subsidy is to be deposited to a welfare fund for remitter. The amount deposited to the fund along with the profit would be payable to the remitter when he/she quits overseas job, or when he/she intends to finance the business of any of his heirs. Such a subsidy would be a goodwill gesture from the government for the remitters and would help remitters to start a business when he/she comes back to the homeland. Since this subsidy would not be directly encashable, it would not affect the current exchange rate.

The last and most important question was; how to utilize the remittances in better way. We have found from the data we collected that the major chunk of investable remittances goes into real estate and in particular, business of plots. This is extremely capital intensive business and we have to replace it with some labor intensive business. We argue that the investable part of remittances can be invested in the mega-development projects using bonds issued in the name of projects. The investors may be paid return when the project become mature. We argue that such an investment must be protected through proper legislation. We also discuss the necessary measures needed to make such investments viable.

publications.title: The Effect of Various Relationship Factors on Business Success; Empirical Evidence from Business Partners of Pakistan and China
publications.author: Prof. Dr. Attiya Yasmin Javid, Shakeel Shahzad, Jawad Ali
publications.description: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment...
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Reports/The Effect of Various Relationship/Cover-image.png

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment in a sample of business partners from Pakistanis and Chinese companies that do business together in Pakistan. Path modeling was used to explore the hierarchical nature of the relationship dimensions amongst one another and on the dependent variables. We conclude that relationship variables in our cross-cultural study are hierarchical and that personal relationships are critical to building and enhancing inter-organizational relationships. We further noted that some relationship dimensions may not have significant direct relationships with commitment, but their indirect and total effects may be significant. Our results challenge conventional conceptualization of relationship dimensions by suggesting a hierarchy of importance among these dimensions.
